text: Amcor plc, originally incorporated as Arctic Jersey Limited under the laws of the Bailiwick of Jersey in July 2018 to facilitate its merger with Bemis Company, Inc., was renamed Amcor plc and became a public limited company under the same jurisdiction on October 10, 2018. On June 11, 2019, Amcor completed the acquisition of Bemis Company, Inc. pursuant to a definitive merger agreement dated August 6, 2018, under which Bemis shareholders received 5.1 Amcor shares for each Bemis share, and Amcor shareholders received one Amcor CHESS Depositary Instrument (CDI) for each Amcor Limited share outstanding. Following the transaction, Amcor shares were registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol "AMCR," while CDIs were traded on the Australian Securities Exchange under the symbol "AMC." Amcor Limited shares were delisted from the ASX, and Bemis shares were delisted from the NYSE. The Company’s business strategy centers on a focused portfolio of strong businesses in flexible and rigid packaging, specialty cartons, and closures, driven by a focus on primary packaging for fast-moving consumer goods, favorable industry structures, attractive relative growth, and multiple competitive advantages. This strategy is supported by differentiated capabilities known as "The Amcor Way," including Talent, Commercial Excellence, Operational Leadership, Innovation, and Cash and Capital Discipline. The Company operates two reporting segments under ASC 280: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. As of June 30, 2020, the Flexibles Segment, which employs approximately 40,000 people across 181 manufacturing facilities in 39 countries, accounted for about 78% of consolidated net sales, while the Rigid Packaging Segment, employing approximately 6,000 people at 50 facilities in 11 countries, accounted for about 22% of consolidated net sales. Sales are primarily conducted through a direct sales force with offices and plants in Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region, and no single customer accounted for more than 10% of consolidated net sales in fiscal year 2020; sales to PepsiCo and its subsidiaries were approximately 11.1% and 11.0% in fiscal years 2019 and 2018, respectively, with arrangements aggregated across multiple contracts. The Company competes in highly competitive markets based on service, innovation, quality, and price, with key competitors including AptarGroup, Inc., Ball Corporation, Berry Global Group, Inc., CCL Industries Inc., Crown Holdings, Inc., Graphic Packaging Holding Company, Huhtamaki Oyj, International Paper Company, Mayr-Melnhof Karton AG, O-I Glass, Inc., Sealed Air Corporation, Silgan Holdings Inc., Sonoco Products Company, WestRock Company, and various privately held companies. The Company maintains inventory levels to balance favorable raw material pricing with timely order fulfillment and does not rely on any single supplier for major raw materials such as polymer resins and films, paper, inks, adhesives, aluminum, and chemicals, which are sourced globally. While raw material availability is currently stable, pricing may fluctuate. Amcor owns or licenses U.S. and international patents, trademarks, and trade secrets related to its products, processes, and equipment, which provide a competitive advantage, though the loss of any single patent or license would not have a material adverse effect on overall operations. The Company believes primary packaging remains essential for protecting and preserving food and healthcare products and is subject to environmental, health, and safety laws and regulations.

Holders of the applicable Notes may proceed directly against the applicable Guarantor under the Guarantee if an event of default affecting those Notes occurs, without first proceeding against the Issuer. Under English insolvency law, if a company enters administration or liquidation, the administrator or liquidator may apply to the court for an order—such as setting aside a transaction—to restore the position as if the company had not entered into a transaction at an "undervalue," defined under the UK Insolvency Act 1986, if the transaction occurred within two years of the onset of insolvency. A transaction is at an undervalue if the company makes a gift or receives consideration significantly below the value of what it gives. Courts generally will not intervene if the transaction was in good faith for business purposes and there were reasonable grounds to believe it would benefit the company. Additionally, if a "preference" is given within six months (or two years if to a connected person) of insolvency, the court may set it aside to restore the position as if the preference had not occurred. A preference occurs when a company does something that puts a creditor, surety, or guarantor in a better position during insolvency than they would have been otherwise. Courts will only make such orders if the company was insolvent at the time of the transaction or became insolvent as a result of it, and for preferences, the company must have been influenced by a desire to improve the beneficiary’s position in insolvency, though this is presumed if the beneficiary is a connected person. If a transaction is made at an undervalue with the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach or prejudicing the interests of creditors, the court may set it aside and protect the interests of "victims" of the transaction, with no statutory time limit for claims except relevant limitation periods, and the company need not be insolvent at the time of the transaction or in liquidation. Under Australian insolvency laws, a guarantee may not be enforceable if a court finds that the guarantor was insolvent at the time of providing the guarantee or became insolvent as a result, or if, upon application of a liquidator, winding up has begun within four years of the guarantee’s issuance and the guarantee is deemed an "uncommercial transaction" under the Australian Act, based on whether a reasonable person in the guarantor’s position would have issued it after considering the benefits, detriments, benefits to other parties, and other relevant facts. Under U.S. bankruptcy law and state fraudulent transfer laws, a guarantee may be voided or claims subordinated if the guarantor at the time of incurrence: (1) intended to hinder, delay, or defraud a creditor or received less than reasonably equivalent value or fair consideration; (2) was insolvent or rendered insolvent by the incurrence; (3) was engaged in a business or transaction with unreasonably small capital relative to its remaining assets; or (4) intended or believed it would incur debts beyond its ability to pay as they mature. Any payments under the guarantee may be voided and returned to the guarantor or to a creditor fund. Insolvency under fraudulent transfer laws generally means: (1) the sum of debts, including contingent liabilities, exceeds the fair saleable value of all assets; (2) the present fair saleable value of assets is less than the amount needed to pay existing debts as they mature; or (3) the guarantor cannot pay its debts as they become due. Under Jersey law, under Article 17 of the Bankruptcy (Désastre) (Jersey) Law 1990 and Article 176 of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may set aside a guarantee entered into at an undervalue if the company’s property is declared "en désastre" or undergoing creditors' winding up, with a five-year look-back period from the commencement of winding up or declaration. If the transaction is found to be at an undervalue, the court may restore the position as if it had not occurred. The Viscount of Jersey or liquidator must prove insolvency unless the beneficiary is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption of insolvency and the connected person must prove otherwise. Under Article 17A and Article 176A, the court may set aside a preference (including a guarantee) given to any person, with a 12-month look-back period. A guarantee constitutes a preference if it puts a creditor or guarantor in a better position during insolvency than they would have been otherwise. If the court finds such a preference, it has wide powers to restore the position. However, it must be shown that the company was influenced by a desire to produce the preferential effect; in proceedings, the Viscount or liquidator must prove insolvency and the desire to create the preference, unless the beneficiary is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption of such desire and the connected person must prove otherwise. In addition to statutory provisions, Jersey customary law, such as a Pauline action, may allow setting aside asset dispositions intended to defeat creditor claims. ### 🔍 ACTIVE RECALL SCENARIOS (BY POLICY)

---

#### 📌 1. **Interest Income – Average Daily Balance Method**
> *Policy: "Interest on Card Member loans is assessed using the average daily balance method. Unless the loan is classified as non-accrual, interest is recognized based upon the principal amount outstanding, in accordance with the terms of the applicable account agreement, until the outstanding balance is paid, or written off."*

**Scenario:**  
*A Card Member has a $10,000 balance on their credit card. They make a $2,000 payment on Day 10 of the billing cycle, and no further transactions occur. The annual interest rate is 18%. What is the interest recognized for the month?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- Use the **average daily balance method**.  
- Days with balance:  
  - Days 1–9: $10,000 × 9 days = $90,000  
  - Days 10–30: $8,000 × 21 days = $168,000  
- Total balance = $258,000  
- Average daily balance = $258,000 / 30 = **$8,600**  
- Monthly interest = $8,600 × (18% / 12) = **$129**  
- ✅ **Answer: $129**

> 💡 *You must recall that interest is based on average daily balance, not just ending balance — and that it stops accruing only if the loan is non-accrual or written off.*

---

#### 📌 2. **Goodwill Impairment – Qualitative vs. Quantitative Assessment**
> *Policy: "We evaluate goodwill for impairment annually as of June 30... We have the option to perform a qualitative assessment... If it is more likely than not that fair value < carrying value, we perform a quantitative assessment using discounted cash flows and market multiples."*

**Scenario:**  
*The company’s CEO reports that the economy has weakened, consumer spending has dropped, and the market value of one of the reporting units has declined. The unit’s carrying value is $500 million, and management believes it is now more likely than not that fair value is below this amount. What steps must be taken?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- Step 1: Perform a **qualitative assessment** of economic conditions, market trends, and financial performance.  
- Step 2: If it is **more likely than not** that fair value < carrying value → proceed to **quantitative assessment**.  
- Step 3: Use **discounted cash flows (income approach)** and **market multiples (market approach)** to estimate fair value.  
- Step 4: If carrying value > fair value → recognize an **impairment loss** equal to the difference.  
- ✅ **Answer: A quantitative goodwill impairment test must be performed, and an impairment loss recognized if fair value is less than carrying value.**

> 💡 *You must recall that qualitative assessment is a shortcut — only if it leads to a "more likely than not" indication of impairment do we go to the detailed model.*

---

#### 📌 3. **Card Member Loans & Receivables – Past Due Status**
> *Policy: "Generally, a Card Member account is considered past due if payment due is not received within 30 days after the billing statement date."*

**Scenario:**  
*A Card Member’s statement was issued on March 1. They were due to pay $1,000 on March 31. They made a payment of $500 on April 10. When is the account considered past due?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- Past due = **after 30 days from billing date**.  
- Billing date: March 1 → 30 days later = April 1.  
- Payment made on April 10 → **after April 1** → account is **past due**.  
- ✅ **Answer: The account is past due as of April 1. It becomes past due on April 1 and remains so until paid.**

> 💡 *You must recall that past due status starts at 30 days post-billing — not when payment is missed, but when the due date passes.*

---

#### 📌 4. **Reserves for Credit Losses – CECL Methodology**
> *Policy: "Effective January 1, 2020, we adopted the CECL methodology... resulting in an increase in reserves for total loans and receivables credit losses."*

**Scenario:**  
*At the end of Q1 2024, management estimates that 2% of all outstanding Card Member loans (totaling $10 billion) are expected to default in the next 12 months. What action should be taken under CECL?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- Under CECL, **reserves are estimated based on expected credit losses** over the life of the loan.  
- Calculate expected loss = $10 billion × 2% = **$200 million**.  
- This amount is recorded as a **reserve for credit losses** (net of any recoveries).  
- ✅ **Answer: A $200 million reserve for credit losses must be established under CECL, reflecting expected losses over the remaining life of the loans.**

> 💡 *You must recall that CECL is prospective and based on **expected losses**, not just incurred losses — and it applies to all loans and receivables.*

---

#### 📌 5. **Leases – Right-of-Use Assets & Liabilities**
> *Policy: "We have operating leases worldwide... leases with terms >12 months are recorded as lease-related assets and liabilities. Lease liabilities are recognized at the present value of contractual fixed payments, discounted using our incremental borrowing rate."*

**Scenario:**  
*American Express signs a 10-year lease for a headquarters building. The annual lease payment is $1 million, and the lease starts on January 1, 2024. The company’s incremental borrowing rate is 5%. What is the lease liability at inception?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- Use **present value of an annuity** at 5% over 10 years.  
- PV factor for 10-year annuity at 5% = 7.7217  
- Lease liability = $1 million × 7.7217 = **$7.72 million**  
- ✅ **Answer: The lease liability is $7.72 million. A right-of-use asset of the same amount is recognized.**

> 💡 *You must recall that lease liabilities are discounted using the **incremental borrowing rate**, and both assets and liabilities are recognized at lease commencement.*

---

#### 📌 6. **Processed Revenue – Network Fees & Issuer Rates**
> *Policy: "We settle with merchants and third-party acquirers on behalf of network partners. The amount of fees charged for accepting American Express-branded cards is generally deducted from the payment and recorded as Processed revenue at the time of transaction."*

**Scenario:**  
*A merchant in the U.S. uses American Express for transactions. The merchant receives $100 from a customer. American Express charges a 2% network fee. The issuer (e.g., a bank) has a negotiated issuer rate of 1.5%. How is the revenue recorded?*

✅ **Active Recall Answer (Apply the rule):**  
- The **network fee (2%)** is deducted from the merchant’s payment → recorded as **Processed revenue**.  
- The **issuer rate (1.5%)** is a contra-revenue (offset) because it’s a fee paid to the issuer.  
- So:  
  - Processed revenue = $100 × (2% - 1.5%) = $0.50  
  - Or: $100 × 2% = $2 → $2 - $1.5 = **$0.50**  
- ✅ **Answer: $0.50 is recorded as Processed revenue (net of issuer rate).**

> 💡 *You must recall that issuer rates are recorded as **contra-revenue**, not revenue — they reduce the total revenue.*

| Judgment Point | Description | Type of Judgment |

| 1. Determination of R&S Period | Choosing a 3-year period beyond the balance sheet date to estimate expected credit losses; assumes long-term average loss rates beyond this period. | Quantitative + Qualitative |

| 3. Allocation of future payments to balances | Allocating future customer payments between interest, fees, spend, and outstanding balances; complex due to revolving nature of loans. | Quantitative + Qualitative |

## 📌 Key Takeaways from the "Judgment Highlight" Technique

✅ **Accounting estimates are not mechanical** — they rely heavily on **assumptions, models, and qualitative inputs**.  
✅ **Management judgment is embedded throughout** the estimation process — from choosing time horizons to interpreting economic scenarios.  
✅ **Sensitivity analyses are illustrative, not predictive** — they highlight risk but do not reflect management’s actual expectations.  
✅ **Qualitative components are essential** — especially for capturing unexpected events, trends, or behavioral shifts.  
✅ **Oversight is required** — these judgments must be reviewed regularly by governance bodies (e.g., Audit Committee, Risk Committee) to ensure transparency and accountability.

---

## 🔁 How to Apply This Strategy Going Forward

1. **Review all accounting estimates** in financial statements or disclosures using this technique.
2. **Create a judgment list** for each estimate — identify the key assumptions and areas of subjectivity.
3. **Map each judgment point** to a governance or oversight body (e.g., Audit Committee, Risk Committee).
4. **Review the list quarterly** to assess whether assumptions have changed or whether new risks have emerged.
5. **Document the rationale** behind key judgments in internal reports or disclosures to enhance transparency.

---

## Final Note

This "Judgment Highlight" technique transforms passive reading of financial disclosures into **active risk and governance analysis**. It ensures that users — investors, auditors, regulators — understand that **accounting estimates are not just numbers, but informed judgments** shaped by economic forecasts, customer behavior, and management discretion.

By applying this method, you move beyond surface-level financial analysis to **deep, insightful understanding of the drivers behind financial reporting**.

│  - Growth in receivables → ↑ securitization → ↓ funding cost    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## ✅ Strategic Takeaways from the Flowchart

1. **Diversification is key** — the mix of deposit, debt, securitization, and secured facilities reduces exposure to any single risk.
2. **FDIC-insured deposits act as a buffer** — they reduce the impact of credit rating downgrades.
3. **CET1 ratio is a critical control point** — stress test result (7%) ensures compliance with key facilities.
4. **Securitization is a low-cost, stable funding tool** — but performance of receivables is a hidden risk.
5. **No single source is fully resilient** — all are vulnerable to market, regulatory, or economic shocks.
6. **Backstop facilities (bank credit, Fed window) are essential** — especially during stress scenarios.

---

## 📌 Final Recommendation

> **To strengthen liquidity resilience**, the company should:
> - Monitor credit ratings closely and maintain a **buffer of secured funding** (e.g., $5B+ in committed facilities)  
> - Maintain **strong receivables quality** to support securitization and collateral  
> - Ensure **CET1 remains above 6.5%** to avoid covenant breaches  
> - Use **stress testing scenarios** to simulate funding disruptions and adjust liquidity buffers accordingly

**Develop a model for the three key credit loss components (PD, EAD, Recovery) with real-world examples**

## 🔹 1. Probability of Default (PD) Model

### 📌 Definition:
PD estimates the likelihood that a borrower will fail to meet their repayment obligations (i.e., default) within a given time period. It is a forward-looking probability based on historical data and current economic conditions.

### 📌 Model Structure:
> **PD = f(Unemployment Rate, GDP Growth, Customer Tenure, Credit Bureau Scores, Delinquency History)**  
> *Weighted by macroeconomic scenarios and portfolio-specific risk factors*

### 📌 Real-World Example (from document):
> In **Q4 2022**, the U.S. unemployment rate rose to **4%**, and GDP growth was projected to contract by **0.1%** (real GDP). These macroeconomic conditions were incorporated into the PD model, leading to a **higher estimated probability of default** across cardmember accounts.  
>  
> This increase in PD directly impacted the overall credit loss reserve, as higher default likelihoods raised the expected losses in the portfolio. For instance, the **Card Member loans reserve increased in 2022** — primarily due to **higher delinquencies and changes in macroeconomic forecasts**, including the elevated unemployment rate.

### 📌 Interdependence:
- Higher PD → increases the **expected loss** → drives up the **reserve rate**.
- PD is a key input to the **EAD model** (since more defaults mean more exposure at default).
- PD also influences **recovery expectations**, as defaults occurring in downturns may have lower recovery rates.

> 💡 *PD acts as the "trigger" — it tells the model when a default is likely, setting the stage for EAD and recovery calculations.*

---

## 🔹 2. Exposure at Default (EAD) Model

### 📌 Definition:
EAD estimates the **balance of a loan or receivable at the time of default**, after accounting for expected repayments. It reflects how much money is still owed when a customer stops paying — and is especially complex in revolving portfolios (like credit cards), where spending and payment behavior vary.

### 📌 Model Structure:
> **EAD = Outstanding Balance – Expected Repayments**  
> *Expected repayments are derived from historical payment behavior, spend patterns, and revolving activity*  
>  
> **EAD = f(Spend Behavior, Payment History, Tenure, Delinquency Status, Credit Score)**

### 📌 Real-World Example (from document):
> In **Q1 2023**, the company observed a shift in **customer spending behavior** due to rising unemployment. The EAD model adjusted downward for accounts with low credit bureau scores and high revolving balances, as these customers were more likely to **increase spending** but **reduce payments**.  
>  
> For example, during a period of economic stress, a customer with a high revolving balance and poor payment history may spend more (due to financial strain), but pay less — leading to a **higher EAD** than expected. This increased exposure at default raised the **expected credit loss** and contributed to the **increase in the receivables reserve** in 2022.

### 📌 Interdependence:
- EAD is **directly influenced by PD** — if PD increases, more accounts default, and EAD becomes more relevant.
- EAD is a **key input to the reserve calculation** — higher EAD = higher expected loss.
- Recovery is applied **after** default, so EAD determines the **amount to recover**.

> 💡 *EAD acts as the "size" of the loss — it tells us how much is at risk when a default happens.*

---

## 🔹 3. Recovery Model

### 📌 Definition:
Recovery estimates the **amount of money expected to be collected from a defaulted account** after the default occurs — typically through collection efforts. It depends on the **timing of default**, **how long it has been past due**, and **macroeconomic conditions**.

### 📌 Model Structure:
> **Recovery Rate = f(Time Since Default, Macroeconomic Conditions, Account Type, Collection Efforts)**  
>  
> *Example: A default in Q4 2022 with 60 days past due may have a 30% recovery rate, while a default in Q1 2023 with 180 days past due may have only 10% due to economic downturn.*

### 📌 Real-World Example (from document):
> In **Q4 2022**, the company modeled recovery rates for accounts written off after **180 days past due**. Due to the **elevated unemployment rate (4%)** and **contracted GDP growth**, the recovery model projected **lower recovery rates** — especially for accounts with long delinquency histories.  
>  
> For instance, a cardmember account written off in Q4 2022 had a **recovery rate of only 15%** (down from 30% in prior years), due to reduced consumer spending and limited ability to repay. This lower recovery rate **increased the net credit loss** (since less is recovered), contributing to the **increase in the loans reserve**.

> Additionally, the document notes that **recovery is estimated for previously written-off accounts**, considering how long ago they were written off — meaning older defaults may be re-evaluated under new economic conditions.

### 📌 Interdependence:
- Recovery **reduces** the final credit loss — so **lower recovery = higher net loss**.
- Recovery is **influenced by PD and EAD** — if a default happens (PD), and the exposure is large (EAD), then recovery becomes a critical factor in determining the final loss.
- Recovery is used to **adjust the reserve rate** — if recovery is high, less reserve is needed.

> 💡 *Recovery acts as the "capping" factor — it tells us how much of the loss can be recovered, shaping the final reserve.*

---

## 🔗 Interdependence Summary: How the Three Models Shape the Reserve Rate

| Component | Role in Reserve Rate | Real-World Impact from Document |
|--------|------------------------|-------------------------------|
| **PD** | Sets the likelihood of default → triggers loss | Higher unemployment (4% in Q4 2022) → higher PD → higher reserve |
| **EAD** | Determines the size of the loss at default | Spending spikes + poor payment behavior → higher EAD → higher reserve |
| **Recovery** | Reduces the net loss after default | Economic downturn → lower recovery → higher net loss → higher reserve |

> ✅ **Collectively**, these three models form a **dynamic, forward-looking credit loss reserve system**:
> - PD identifies *when* defaults happen  
> - EAD determines *how much* is at risk  
> - Recovery determines *how much* can be recovered  
>  
> The **reserve rate** = (PD × EAD × (1 – Recovery Rate))  
> This formula is not explicitly stated, but it is **implied** in the document’s logic.

---

## 📌 Final Insight: Why This Matters

The document shows that **reserves are not static** — they are **dynamically adjusted** based on:
- Real-time macroeconomic data (unemployment, GDP)
- Historical portfolio behavior (delinquency, spend, payment patterns)
- Judgment calls (qualitative reserves for emerging trends)

For example:
- In **2022**, higher unemployment → higher PD → higher EAD → lower recovery → **reserve increased**
- In **2021**, improved unemployment forecasts → lower PD → lower reserve

This demonstrates that **the three models are interdependent and form a feedback loop** that continuously updates the credit loss reserve in response to changing economic and behavioral conditions.

---

## ✅ Learning Outcome

By building these **simple, real-world models** using data from the document, you now understand:
- How **PD, EAD, and Recovery** are not isolated metrics but **interconnected pillars** of credit risk modeling.
- How **macroeconomic variables** (like unemployment and GDP) directly influence each component.
- How **real-world decisions** (e.g., reserve increases/decreases) reflect the combined output of these models.

This internalization helps in **practicing financial modeling**, **understanding credit risk frameworks**, and **evaluating reserve adequacy** in real-world financial statements.

text: Amcor’s obligations to pay Additional Amounts, if and when due, will survive the termination of the indenture and the payment of all other amounts in respect of the Notes. Any mention of a payment of or in respect of the principal of, or any premium or interest on, the Notes (or payments pursuant to the Guarantees thereof) shall be deemed to include payment of Additional Amounts to the extent such Additional Amounts are, were, or would be payable under the indenture in such context, and any express mention of Additional Amounts in the indenture shall not exclude such amounts where such mention is not made. Certain additional amounts may be payable in respect of the Notes and Guarantees as a result of consolidations or mergers involving, or conveyances, transfers, or leases of properties and assets by the Issuer or the Guarantors, as set out in “—Certain covenants—Consolidation, merger and sale of assets.” If, as a result of (a) any change in or amendment to the laws, regulations, published practice, or published tax rulings of any Relevant Jurisdiction, or of any political subdivision or taxing authority thereof, affecting taxation, or (b) any change in the official administration, application, or interpretation by a relevant court or tribunal, government, or government authority of such laws, regulations, published practice, or published tax rulings—either generally or in relation to the Notes or the Guarantees—becoming effective on or after the later of (x) the original issue date of the Notes or the Guarantees or (y) the date on which a jurisdiction becomes a Relevant Jurisdiction (by consolidation, merger, or transfer of assets of the Issuer or any Guarantor, change in place of payment on the Notes or any Guarantee, or otherwise), or which change in official administration, application, or interpretation was not available to the public prior to such later date, the Issuer or the applicable Guarantor would be required to pay Additional Amounts in respect of interest on the next succeeding interest payment date (assuming, in the case of the Guarantors, a payment in respect of such interest was required to be made by the applicable Guarantor under the Guarantee thereof on such interest payment date and the applicable Guarantor would be unable, for reasons outside their control, to procure payment by the Issuer), and such obligation cannot be avoided by the use of commercially reasonable measures available to the Issuer or the applicable Guarantor. In such case, the Issuer may, at its option, redeem all (but not less than all) of the corresponding Notes upon not less than 30 nor more than 60 days' written notice as provided in the indenture: (i) in the case of Notes represented by a global note, to and through Euroclear or Clearstream for communication by them to the holders of interests in the Notes to be so redeemed, or (ii) in the case of definitive Notes, to each holder of record of the Notes to be redeemed at its registered address, at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount thereof plus accrued interest to the date fixed for redemption; provided, however, that: (1) no such notice of redemption may be given earlier than 60 days prior to the earliest date on which the Issuer or the applicable Guarantor would be obligated to pay such Additional Amounts were a payment in respect of the Notes or the applicable Guarantee thereof then due; and (2) at the time any such redemption notice is given, such obligation to pay such Additional Amounts must remain in effect. Prior to any such redemption, the Issuer, the applicable Guarantor, or any Person with whom the Issuer or the applicable Guarantor has consolidated or merged, or to whom the Issuer or the applicable Guarantor has conveyed or transferred or leased all or substantially all of its properties and assets (the successor Person in any such transaction, a "Successor Person"), as the case may be, shall provide the Trustee with an opinion of counsel to the effect that the conditions precedent to such redemption have occurred and a certificate signed by an authorized officer stating that the obligation to pay Additional Amounts cannot be avoided by taking measures that the Issuer, the applicable Guarantor, or the Successor Person, as the case may be, believes are commercially reasonable. The Notes are redeemable, in whole or in part, at the option of the Issuer at any time at a redemption price equal to the greater of (1) 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed and (2) as determined by the Quotation Agent (as defined below), the sum of (a) the present value of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed and (b) the present value of the remaining scheduled payments of interest thereon (not including any portion of such payments of interest accrued to the date of redemption) from the redemption date to the maturity date of the Note being redeemed, in each case, discounted to the date of redemption on an annual basis (Actual/Actual ICMA) at the Comparable Government Bond Rate (as defined below) plus 30 basis points (0.300%), plus, in each case, accrued and unpaid interest thereon to the date of redemption; provided, however, notwithstanding the foregoing, if the Issuer redeems any of the Notes on or after the Par Call Date (as defined below), such Notes are redeemable at the Issuer's option at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed, plus accrued and unpaid interest to the redemption date of such Notes being redeemed to such date of redemption. The principal amount of any Note remaining outstanding after a redemption in part shall be €100,000 or a higher integral multiple of €1,000. Notwithstanding the foregoing, installments of interest on Notes that are due and payable on interest payment dates falling on or prior to a redemption date will be payable on the interest payment date to the registered holders of Notes as of the close of business on the relevant record date according to the Notes and the indenture. "Comparable Government Bond" means, in relation to any Comparable Government Bond Rate calculation, at the discretion of an independent investment bank selected by us (the "Quotation Agent"), a German government bond whose maturity is closest to the par call date, or if such Quotation Agent in its discretion determines that such similar bond is not in issue, such other German government bond as such Quotation Agent may, with the advice of three brokers of, and/or market makers in, German government bonds selected by us, determine to be appropriate for determining the Comparable Government Bond Rate. "Comparable Government Bond Rate" means the price, expressed as a percentage (rounded to three decimal places, with 0.0005 being rounded upwards), at which the gross redemption yield on the Notes to be redeemed, if they were to be purchased at such price on the third Business Day prior to the date fixed for redemption, would be equal to the gross redemption yield on such Business Day of the Comparable Government Bond on the basis of the middle market price of the Comparable Government Bond prevailing at 11:00 A.M. (London time) on such Business Day as determined by the Quotation Agent selected by us. "Par Call Date" means April 23, 2027. Notice of any redemption will be provided at least 30 days but not more than 60 days before the redemption date to each holder of the Notes to be redeemed (i) in the case of Notes represented by a global note, to and through Euroclear or Clearstream for communication by them to the holders of interests in the Notes to be so redeemed, or (ii) in the case of definitive Notes, by mail to each holder of record of the Notes to be redeemed at its registered address. Unless the Issuer defaults in payment of the redemption price and accrued interest, on and after the redemption date, interest will cease to accrue on the Notes or portions thereof called for redemption. If less than all of the Notes are being redeemed, the Notes for redemption will be selected as follows: • if the Notes are held through Euroclear or Clearstream, in compliance with the standard procedures of Euroclear and Clearstream; or • if the Notes are not held through any clearing system, on a pro rata basis, by lot or by such other method as the Trustee deems fair and appropriate. The Trustee may select for redemption the Notes and portions of the Notes in amounts of €100,000 or integral multiples of €1,000 in excess thereof. The indenture and the Notes are governed by, and construed in accordance with, the laws of the State of New York. The Issuer and the Guarantors have commercial deposits and custodial arrangements with Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, or "Deutsche Bank," and may have borrowed money from Deutsche Bank or its affiliates in the normal course of business. The Issuer and the Guarantors may enter into similar or other banking relationships with Deutsche Bank or its affiliates in the future in the normal course of business. Deutsche Bank may also act as trustee with respect to other debt securities issued by the Issuer and the Guarantors. Neither the Issuer nor any of the Guarantors is required to make any sinking fund payments or any offers to purchase with respect to the Notes or the Guarantees. The Issuer or the Guarantors may at any time and from time to time purchase Notes in the open market or otherwise. Pursuant to the indenture, the Issuer and each of the Guarantors have covenanted and agreed as follows. The indenture provides that, upon the occurrence of a Change Of Control Triggering Event, unless the Issuer has exercised its right to redeem the Notes in accordance with their terms, each holder of the Notes will have the right to require the Issuer to purchase all or a portion of such holder's Notes pursuant to the offer described below (the "Change of Control Offer"), at a purchase price equal to 101% of the principal amount thereof plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of purchase, subject to the rights of holders of the Notes on the relevant record date to receive interest due on the relevant interest payment date. Within 30 days following the date upon which the Change of Control Triggering Event occurred, or at the Issuer's option, prior to any Change of Control but after the public announcement of the pending Change of Control, the Issuer will be required to send, by first class mail, a notice to each holder of the Notes, with a copy to the Trustee, which notice will govern the terms of the Change of Control Offer. Such notice will state, among other things, the purchase date, which must be no earlier than 30 days nor later than 60 days from the date such notice is mailed, other than as may be required by law (the "Change of Control Payment Date"). The notice, if mailed prior to the date of consummation of the Change of Control, will state that the Change of Control Offer is conditioned on the Change of Control being consummated on or prior to the Change of Control Payment Date. Holders of Notes electing to have Notes purchased pursuant to a Change of Control Offer will be required to surrender their Notes, with the form entitled "Option of Holder to Elect Purchase" on the reverse of the Note completed, to the Trustee at the address specified in the notice, or transfer their Notes to the Trustee by book-entry transfer pursuant to the applicable procedures of the Trustee, prior to the close of business on the third Business Day prior to the Change of Control Payment Date. The Issuer will not be required to make a Change of Control Offer if a third party makes such an offer in the manner, at the times and otherwise in compliance with the requirements for such an offer made by the Issuer and such third party purchases all corresponding Notes properly tendered and not withdrawn under its offer. The definition of Change of Control includes a phrase relating to the direct or indirect sale, lease, transfer, conveyance, or other disposition of "all or substantially all" of our assets and the assets of our subsidiaries taken as a whole. Although there is a limited body of case law interpreting the phrase "substantially all," there is no precise, established definition of the phrase under applicable law. Accordingly, the applicability of the requirement that the Issuer offer to repurchase the Notes as a result of a sale, lease, transfer, conveyance, or other disposition of less than all of our assets and the assets of our subsidiaries taken as a whole to another "person" (as such terms is used in Section 13(d)(3) of the Exchange Act) may be uncertain. Pursuant to the indenture, for so long as any of the Notes or any of the Guarantees are outstanding, Amcor will not, and will not permit any Subsidiary to, create, assume, incur, issue, or otherwise have outstanding any Lien upon, or with respect to, any of the present or future business, property, undertaking, assets or revenues (including, without limitation, any Equity Interests and uncalled capital), whether now owned or hereafter acquired (together, "assets") of Amcor or such Subsidiary, to secure any Indebtedness, unless the Notes and applicable Guarantees are secured by such Lien equally and ratably with (or prior to) such Indebtedness, except for the following, to which this covenant shall not apply: (a) Liens on assets securing Indebtedness of Amcor or such Subsidiary outstanding on the date of the indenture; (b) Liens on assets securing Indebtedness owing to Amcor or any Subsidiary (other than a Project Subsidiary); (c) Liens existing on any asset prior to the acquisition of such asset by Amcor or any Subsidiary after the original issue date of the Notes, provided that (i) such Lien has not been created in anticipation of such asset being so acquired, (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other asset of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets covered by such Lien on the date of such acquisition of such assets, (iii) such Lien shall secure only the Indebtedness secured by such Lien on the date of such acquisition of such asset and (iv) such Lien shall be discharged within one year of the date of acquisition of such asset or such later date as may be the date of the maturity of the Indebtedness that such Lien secures if such Indebtedness is fixed interest rate indebtedness that provides a commercial financial advantage to Amcor and the Subsidiaries; (d) Liens on any assets of a Person that becomes a Subsidiary (or of any Person not previously a Subsidiary that is merged or consolidated with or into a Subsidiary) after the original issue date of the Notes that existed prior to the time such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated), provided that (i) such Lien has not been created in anticipation of such Person becoming a Subsidiary (or such merger or consolidation), (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other asset of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets covered by such Lien on the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated), (iii) such Lien shall secure only the Indebtedness secured by such Lien on the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated) and (iv) such Lien shall be discharged within one year of the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated) or such later date as may be the date of the maturity of the Indebtedness that such Lien secures if such Indebtedness is fixed interest rate indebtedness that provides a commercial financial advantage to Amcor and the Subsidiaries; (e) Liens created to secure Indebtedness, directly or indirectly, incurred for the purpose of purchasing Equity Interests or other assets (other than real or personal property of the type contemplated by clause (f) below), provided that (i) such Lien shall secure only such Indebtedness incurred for the purpose of purchasing such assets, (ii) such Lien shall apply only to the assets so purchased (and to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, any subsequently after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets so purchased) and (iii) such Lien shall be discharged within two years of such Lien being granted; (f) Liens created to secure Indebtedness incurred for the purpose of acquiring or developing any real or personal property or for some other purpose in connection with the acquisition or development of such property, provided that (i) such Lien shall secure only such Indebtedness, (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other assets of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the property so acquired or developed and (iii) the rights of the holder of the Indebtedness secured by such Lien shall be limited to the property that is subject to such Lien, it being the intention that the holder of such Lien shall not have any recourse to Amcor or any Subsidiaries personally or to any other property of Amcor or any Subsidiary; (g) Liens for any borrowings from any financial institution for the purpose of financing any import or export contract in respect of which any part of the price receivable is guaranteed or insured by such financial institution carrying on an export credit guarantee or insurance business, provided that (i) such Lien applies only to the assets that are the subject of such import or export contract and (ii) the amount of Indebtedness secured thereby does not exceed the amount so guaranteed or insured; (h) Liens for Indebtedness from an international or governmental development agency or authority to finance the development of a specific project.

text: Amcor plc, originally incorporated as Arctic Jersey Limited in July 2018 and renamed Amcor plc on October 10, 2018, is a holding company incorporated under the Laws of the Bailiwick of Jersey. On June 11, 2019, the company completed its acquisition of Bemis Company, Inc., creating a global packaging leader. The Company develops and produces flexible packaging, rigid packaging containers, specialty cartons, and closures, employing approximately 47,000 individuals across 231 manufacturing facilities in over 40 countries. Its business is organized into two reporting segments: Flexibles and Rigid Packaging, with sales diversified across Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, and the Asia Pacific regions, primarily serving the food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical device, home and personal care, and other consumer goods markets. All markets are highly competitive in terms of price, innovation, quality, and service. The consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP and include the accounts of Amcor and its majority-owned subsidiaries, with intercompany transactions and balances eliminated. The Company uses the acquisition method of accounting for business combinations, recognizing assets and liabilities at fair value on the acquisition date, with goodwill measured as the excess of consideration transferred and non-controlling interests over the fair value of net assets acquired. During the measurement period, up to one year from the acquisition date, adjustments to assets and liabilities may be recorded against goodwill. Upon conclusion of the measurement period or final determination of asset and liability values, any subsequent adjustments are recorded in the consolidated statement of income. The three European plants acquired as part of the Bemis acquisition were classified as a discontinued operation in fiscal 2019 due to a divestiture agreement with the European Commission, and were divested in the first quarter of fiscal 2020. The Company’s financial statements require management estimates and assumptions based on historical experience and current beliefs, which are reviewed and adjusted as circumstances change. The impact of the 2019 Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic is considered uncertain and may influence future accounting estimates. Foreign currency translation is applied using average exchange rates for subsidiaries with functional currencies other than the U.S. dollar, with monetary assets and liabilities remeasured at the balance sheet date exchange rate. Foreign currency transaction gains and losses are recorded in other non-operating income (loss), net, or other income, net, depending on the nature of the transaction. The Company recorded a foreign currency transaction net loss of $0.4 million in 2020, a net gain of $1.1 million in 2019, and a net loss of $82.7 million in 2018. The Argentine economy was designated as highly inflationary as of July 1, 2018, resulting in the U.S. dollar becoming the functional currency for subsidiaries in Argentina, with impacts of $27.7 million and $30.2 million in 2020 and 2019, respectively. Revenue is recognized at the point of shipment when control transfers to the customer, net of returns, customer claims, and taxes collected, which are remitted to authorities. The Company does not have material contract assets or liabilities and disaggregates revenue by geography, as detailed in Note 20. The Company determines that packaging is a single performance obligation, as the customer cannot benefit from packaging independently. Variable consideration, such as sales rebates and prompt payment discounts, is accounted for using the most likely amount method based on forecasted sales and rebate percentages. Up-front payments under long-term agreements are deferred and recorded as prepaid expenses or other assets. Contract incentives are recognized as a reduction to revenue over the contract term. External sales commissions are expensed when incurred due to their short amortization period, and shipping and handling costs are classified as cost of products sold, with billed amounts included in net sales. Taxes collected from customers are excluded from net sales. The time value of money is not adjusted for contracts where the payment and performance period is one year or less. Research and development expenses are expensed as incurred. Restructuring costs are recognized when incurred, with severance provisions recorded when probable and estimable, and fixed assets written off when disposal is committed. Other restructuring costs are recorded as incurred or when services are provided. See accompanying notes to consolidated financial statements, including Note 22, "Supplemental Cash Flow Information," Note 3, "New Accounting Guidance," and Note 4, "Acquisitions and Divestitures," for additional details.

The 2018 Rigid Packaging Restructuring Plan is expected to be completed during fiscal year 2021. As part of this plan, eight manufacturing facilities were closed and headcount was reduced at certain facilities. The total pre-tax restructuring costs were $230.8 million, comprising $166.7 million in employee termination costs, $31.4 million in fixed asset impairment costs, and $32.7 million in other costs, primarily for dismantling equipment and terminating existing lease contracts. Approximately $166 million of the $230.8 million in total program costs resulted in cash expenditures, with cash payments for fiscal year 2019 being $14.4 million. The 2016 Flexibles Restructuring Plan was substantially completed by the end of fiscal year 2019. Due to impairment indicators present for the years ended June 30, 2020, 2019, and 2018, the company performed impairment tests by comparing the carrying value of its investment in AMVIG Holdings Limited ("AMVIG") to its fair value, determined using AMVIG's quoted share price. Impairment charges of $25.6 million, $14.0 million, and $36.5 million were recorded in fiscal years 2020, 2019, and 2018, respectively, as the fair value was below the carrying value. The company has subsidiaries in Argentina with a historical functional currency of the Argentine Peso. As of June 30, 2018, the Argentine economy was designated as highly inflationary for accounting purposes, and beginning July 1, 2018, the financial results of the Argentinean subsidiaries were reported using the U.S. dollar as the functional currency of the parent. This transition resulted in a negative impact of $27.7 million and $30.2 million on the consolidated statement of income for the years ended June 30, 2020 and 2019, respectively. Net sales increased by $3,009.3 million, or 31.8%, to $12,467.5 million in fiscal year 2020 from $9,458.2 million in fiscal year 2019. Net income attributable to Amcor plc increased by $182.0 million, or 42.3%, to $612.2 million in fiscal year 2020 from $430.2 million in fiscal year 2019, primarily due to the Bemis acquisition and related transaction and integration cost impacts. Diluted earnings per share ("Diluted EPS") increased to $0.382, or 5.2%, in fiscal year 2020 from $0.363 in fiscal year 2019, with net income attributable to ordinary shareholders rising 42.3% and the diluted weighted average number of shares outstanding increasing 35.3%, driven by the Bemis acquisition. Net sales including intersegment sales in the Flexibles segment increased by $3,188.0 million, or 48.5%, to $9,754.7 million in fiscal year 2020 from $6,566.7 million in fiscal year 2019. Excluding negative currency impacts of $235.2 million (3.6%) and pass-through of lower raw material costs of $87.9 million (1.4%), the increase was $3,511.1 million, or 53.5%, driven by favorable volumes of 0.1% and unfavorable price/mix of (0.1%), with acquisition-related impacts contributing 53.5%. Adjusted EBIT from continuing operations in the Flexibles segment increased by $517.9 million, or 63.4%, to $1,335.1 million in fiscal year 2020 from $817.2 million in fiscal year 2019. Excluding negative currency impacts of $25.4 million (3.0%), the increase was $543.3 million, or 66.4%, driven by plant cost improvements of 8.7%, SG&A and other cost improvements of 2.5%, favorable volumes of 0.1%, partially offset by unfavorable price/mix of (1.5%), with acquisition-related impacts contributing 56.6%. Net sales in the Rigid Packaging segment decreased by $176.4 million, or 6.1%, to $2,716.3 million in fiscal year 2020 from $2,892.7 million in fiscal year 2019. Excluding negative currency impacts of $39.0 million (1.3%) and pass-through of lower raw material costs of $117.7 million (4.1%), the decrease was $19.7 million, or 0.7%, driven by favorable volumes of 0.5% and unfavorable price/mix of (1.2%). Adjusted EBIT for the Rigid Packaging segment decreased by $18.1 million, or 5.9%, to $290.1 million in fiscal year 2020 from $308.2 million in fiscal year 2019. Excluding negative currency impacts of $5.1 million (1.7%), the decrease was $13.0 million, or 4.2%, driven by favorable plant costs of 2.2%, favorable SG&A and other costs at 0.9%, favorable volumes of 0.4%, and unfavorable price/mix of 7.7%. Consolidated gross profit increased by $736.4 million, or 40.9%, to $2,535.5 million in fiscal year 2020 from $1,799.1 million in fiscal year 2019, primarily driven by the Bemis acquisition in the Flexibles segment. Consolidated SG&A expenses increased by $385.8 million, or 38.6%, to $1,384.8 million in fiscal year 2020 from $999.0 million in fiscal year 2019, primarily in the Flexibles segment and Other, driven by the Bemis acquisition, including related transaction and integration cost impacts. R&D expenses increased by $33.3 million, or 52.0%, to $97.3 million in fiscal year 2020 from $64.0 million in fiscal year 2019, primarily due to the addition of the Bemis cost base and timing of project costs. Restructuring and related expenses decreased by $15.7 million to $115.1 million in fiscal year 2020 from $130.8 million in fiscal year 2019, primarily due to a reduction in restructuring activities related to the 2018 Rigid Packaging Restructuring Plan. Other income, net decreased by $130.7 million to $55.7 million in fiscal year 2020 from $186.4 million in fiscal year 2019, mainly due to the nonrecurrence of remedy disposal related gains in fiscal year 2019. Interest income increased by $5.4 million, or 32.1%, to $22.2 million in fiscal year 2020 from $16.8 million in fiscal year 2019, mainly driven by higher cash balances and negative interest rates on Euro-denominated borrowings. Interest expense remained relatively stable at $206.9 million in fiscal year 2020 compared to $207.9 million in fiscal year 2019. Other non-operating income, net increased by $12.4 million to $15.9 million in fiscal year 2020 from $3.5 million in fiscal year 2019, mainly driven by impacts related to the acquired Bemis pension plans. Contingencies in Brazil involve various governmental assessments and litigation, primarily related to excise and income tax claims. The Company vigorously defends these positions and believes it will prevail on most, if not all, matters. The ultimate resolution is not expected to materially impact consolidated results of operations, financial position, or cash flows. Under local regulations, Brazilian subsidiaries may need to post cash or collateral if a challenge proceeds to court; however, the level of cash or collateral already pledged or potentially required would not significantly impact liquidity. The litigation process is subject to many uncertainties, and the outcome of individual matters cannot be accurately predicted. The Company assesses these matters for the probability of incurring a liability and records the best estimate of the ultimate loss where the likelihood is probable. The assessments are based on knowledge and experience, but the ultimate outcome may differ from estimates. As of June 30, 2023, the Company provided letters of credit of $16 million, judicial insurance of $2 million, and deposited cash of $14 million with courts to defend these cases. Contingencies related to environmental matters include the Company being identified as a potentially responsible party ("PRP") at several waste disposal sites under U.S. federal and related state environmental statutes and regulations, potentially facing material environmental remediation obligations. While the Company benefits from various insurance policies, actual coverage may not, or only partially, cover total potential exposures. As of June 30, 2023, the Company has recorded aggregate accruals of $9 million for its share of estimated future remediation costs at these sites. In addition, the Company has recorded aggregate accruals of $54 million for potential liabilities for remediation obligations at various worldwide locations that are owned or operated by the Company or were formerly owned or operated. The SEC requires disclosure of environmental proceedings that may result in monetary sanctions above a $1 million threshold; applying this threshold, there are no environmental matters required to be disclosed for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023. While the Company believes its accruals are adequate, there can be no assurance that ultimate payments will not exceed accrued amounts. Based on available information, the Company does not believe its potential environmental obligations will have a material adverse effect on liquidity, results of operations, or financial condition. text: Under Article 17A of the Jersey Bankruptcy Law and Article 176A of the Jersey Companies Law, the court may, upon application by the Viscount of Jersey (in the case of a company whose property has been declared "en désastre") or the liquidator (in the case of a creditors' winding up), set aside a preference—such as a guarantee—given by the company to any individual. This applies within a 12-month look-back period beginning from the date of the commencement of the winding up or the declaration of "désastre," during which guarantees are subject to examination. A guarantee will be considered a preference if it places a creditor of the Jersey company—or a surety or guarantor for any of the company’s debts or liabilities—in a better position than they would have been had the transaction not occurred, in the event of the company’s insolvency. If the court finds that the guarantee constituted such a preference, it has broad powers to restore the financial position to what it would have been absent the preference. However, for such a restoration to occur, it must be proven that the company acted with a desire to produce the preferential effect. In proceedings, it is the responsibility of the Viscount of Jersey or the liquidator to establish that the company was insolvent at the relevant time and that it was motivated by a desire to create a preferential outcome, unless the beneficiary of the guarantee is a connected person, in which case there is a presumption that the company acted with such a desire, and the connected person must prove otherwise. In addition to these statutory provisions, Jersey customary law principles—such as a Pauline action—may also allow for the setting aside of asset dispositions intended to defeat creditor claims. The document also includes a series of defined terms, including "Accounts," which refers to consolidated financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP, along with related reports and notes; "Australian Act," meaning the Corporations Act 2001 (Cwlth); "Business Day," defined as any day when banking institutions in New York or London are open and the TARGET2 system is operational; "Change in Lease Accounting Standard," referring to the effectiveness of FASB ASC 842 or AASB AAS 16; "Change of Control," defined as the sale or transfer of all or substantially all of Amcor’s assets, a change in beneficial ownership exceeding 50% of voting stock, a merger or consolidation resulting in a change of control, the resignation of a majority of the board, or the adoption of a liquidation plan; "Change of Control Trigger Period," which begins on the earlier of the occurrence of a Change of Control or 60 days before its public announcement and ends 60 days after consummation, with possible extension if any Rating Agency publicly announces a possible ratings change; "Change of Control Triggering Event," which occurs if two or more of the Rating Agencies engaged by Amcor or Amcor UK cease to rate the Notes as Investment Grade during the Trigger Period, or if there are fewer than two Rating Agencies providing ratings at the start of the period; "Continuing Director," defined as a board member present at the time of the Notes issuance or elected with majority approval of existing Continuing Directors; "Default," meaning any event that constitutes or would become an Event of Default; "Equity Interests," including shares, partnership interests, and rights to purchase equity, excluding convertible debt securities prior to conversion; "Finance Lease," as defined under U.S. GAAP FASB ASC 840; "Fitch," a rating agency; "Group," meaning Amcor and its Subsidiaries taken together; "Hedge Agreement," defined as any derivative or swap transaction, excluding employee share or bonus plan options or phantom rights; "Indebtedness," encompassing all obligations in respect of borrowed money, guarantees, lease liabilities, hedging obligations, redeemable preferred shares, letters of credit, deferred payments, factored debts, and other financial instruments, including those of related entities to the extent of liability; "Investment Grade," defined as a rating of Baa3 or better by Moody’s, BBB- or better by S&P or Fitch, or an equivalent rating by a Substitute Rating Agency; "Lien," including mortgages, security interests, and vendor or lessor interests under conditional sale agreements or finance leases, excluding normal commercial title retention; "Limited Recourse Indebtedness," for financing projects, where the relevant party has limited recourse to Amcor or its Subsidiaries except through a Lien on Project Assets; "Moody’s," a rating agency; "Person," any individual or entity; "Project," any acquisition, development, or exploitation of assets; "Project Assets," assets directly related to a Project or proposed Project, or fully paid shares in a Subsidiary engaged solely in that Project with no recourse beyond those shares; "Rating Agency," including Moody’s, S&P, Fitch, or a Substitute Rating Agency engaged by Amcor; "S&P," a rating agency; "Specified Indebtedness," meaning debt of at least $150,000,000 issued under a credit facility or similar agreement; "Subsidiary," any entity in which Amcor or a Subsidiary controls a majority of voting interests or owns more than 50% of profits or capital, unless it operates independently; "Substitute Rating Agency," a nationally recognized statistical rating organization engaged by Amcor when Moody’s, S&P, or Fitch cease providing ratings; and "Total Tangible Assets," defined as the sum of the Group’s tangible assets minus the lesser of the aggregate value of all Project Assets subject to certain conditions.

answer: (a) Liens on assets securing Indebtedness of Amcor or such Subsidiary outstanding on the date of the indenture; (b) Liens on assets securing Indebtedness owing to Amcor or any Subsidiary (other than a Project Subsidiary); (c) Liens existing on any asset prior to the acquisition of such asset by Amcor or any Subsidiary after the original issue date of the Notes, provided that (i) such Lien has not been created in anticipation of such asset being so acquired, (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other asset of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets covered by such Lien on the date of such acquisition of such assets, (iii) such Lien shall secure only the Indebtedness secured by such Lien on the date of such acquisition of such asset and (iv) such Lien shall be discharged within one year of the date of acquisition of such asset or such later date as may be the date of the maturity of the Indebtedness that such Lien secures if such Indebtedness is fixed interest rate indebtedness that provides a commercial financial advantage to Amcor and the Subsidiaries; (d) Liens on any assets of a Person that becomes a Subsidiary (or of any Person not previously a Subsidiary that is merged or consolidated with or into a Subsidiary) after the original issue date of the Notes that existed prior to the time such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated), provided that (i) such Lien has not been created in anticipation of such Person becoming a Subsidiary (or such merger or consolidation), (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other asset of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets covered by such Lien on the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated), (iii) such Lien shall secure only the Indebtedness secured by such Lien on the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated) and (iv) such Lien shall be discharged within one year of the date such Person becomes a Subsidiary (or is so merged or consolidated) or such later date as may be the date of the maturity of the Indebtedness that such Lien secures if such Indebtedness is fixed interest rate indebtedness that provides a commercial financial advantage to Amcor and the Subsidiaries; (e) Liens created to secure Indebtedness, directly or indirectly, incurred for the purpose of purchasing Equity Interests or other assets (other than real or personal property of the type contemplated by clause (f) below), provided that (i) such Lien shall secure only such Indebtedness incurred for the purpose of purchasing such assets, (ii) such Lien shall apply only to the assets so purchased (and to proceeds and products of, and, in the case of any assets other than Equity Interests, any subsequently after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the assets so purchased) and (iii) such Lien shall be discharged within two years of such Lien being granted; (f) Liens created to secure Indebtedness incurred for the purpose of acquiring or developing any real or personal property or for some other purpose in connection with the acquisition or development of such property, provided that (i) such Lien shall secure only such Indebtedness, (ii) such Lien shall not apply to any other assets of Amcor or any Subsidiary, other than to proceeds and products of, and after-acquired property that is affixed or incorporated into, the property so acquired or developed and (iii) the rights of the holder of the Indebtedness secured by such Lien shall be limited to the property that is subject to such Lien, it being the intention that the holder of such Lien shall not have any recourse to Amcor or any Subsidiaries personally or to any other property of Amcor or any Subsidiary; (g) Liens for any borrowings from any financial institution for the purpose of financing any import or export contract in respect of which any part of the price receivable is guaranteed or insured by such financial institution carrying on an export credit guarantee or insurance business, provided that (i) such Lien applies only to the assets that are the subject of such import or export contract and (ii) the amount of Indebtedness secured thereby does not exceed the amount so guaranteed or insured; (h) Liens for Indebtedness from an international or governmental development agency or authority to finance the development of a specific project, provided that (i) such Lien is required by applicable law or practice and (ii) the Lien is created only over assets used in or derived from the development of such project; (i) any Lien created in favor of co-venturers of Amcor or any Subsidiary pursuant to any agreement relating to an unincorporated joint venture, provided that (i) such Lien applies only to the Equity Interests in, or the assets of, such unincorporated joint venture and (ii) such Lien secures solely the payment of obligations arising under such agreement; (j) Liens over goods and products, or documents of title to goods and products, arising in the ordinary course of business in connection with letters of credit and similar transactions, provided that such Liens secure only the acquisition cost or selling price (and amounts incidental thereto) of such goods and products required to be paid within 180 days; (k) Liens arising by operation of law in the ordinary course of business of Amcor or any Subsidiary; (l) Liens created by Amcor or any Subsidiary over a Project Asset of Amcor or such Subsidiary, provided that such Lien secures only (i) in the case of a Lien over assets referred to in clause (a) of the definition of Project Assets, Limited Recourse Indebtedness incurred by Amcor or such Subsidiary or (ii) in the case of a Lien over Equity Interests referred to in clause (b) of the definition of Project Assets, Limited Recourse Indebtedness incurred by the direct Subsidiary of Amcor or such Subsidiary; (m) Liens arising under any netting or set-off arrangement entered into by Amcor or any Subsidiary in the ordinary course of its banking arrangements for the purpose of netting debit and credit balances of Amcor or any Subsidiary; (n) Liens incurred in connection with any extension, renewal, replacement or refunding (together, a "refinancing") of any Lien permitted in clauses (a) through (m) above and any successive refinancings thereof permitted by this clause (n) (each an "Existing Security"), provided that (i) such Liens do not extend to any asset that was not expressed to be subject to the Existing Security, (ii) the principal amount of Indebtedness secured by such Liens does not exceed the principal amount of Indebtedness that was outstanding and secured by the Existing Security at the time of such refinancing and (iii) any refinancing of an Existing Security incurred in accordance with clauses (c) through (e) above (and any subsequent refinancings thereof permitted by this clause (n)) will not affect the obligation to discharge such Liens within the time frames that applied to such Existing Security at the time it was first incurred (as specified in the applicable clause); (o) any Lien arising as a result of a Change in Lease Accounting Standard; and (p) other Liens by Amcor or any Subsidiary securing Indebtedness, provided that, immediately after giving effect to the incurrence or assumption of any such Lien or the incurrence of any Indebtedness secured thereby, the aggregate principal amount of all outstanding Indebtedness of Amcor and any Subsidiary secured by any Liens pursuant to this clause (p) shall not exceed 10% of Total Tangible Assets at such time

The Company uses derivatives and other financial instruments to hedge exposures to interest rate, commodity price, and currency risks without holding or issuing them for speculative or trading purposes. For hedges meeting the hedge accounting criteria, the Company formally designates and documents them as either fair value hedges or cash flow hedges of specific underlying exposures and continuously assesses and documents their effectiveness. To manage interest rate risk, the Company maintains a mix of fixed-rate and variable-rate debt, monitors global interest rates, and hedges floating interest rate exposure through instruments such as interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, and interest rate locks. For interest rate swaps designated as fair value hedges, gains and losses on changes in fair value are included in interest expense and offset changes in the fair value of the hedged debt due to market interest rate changes. Gains or losses on interest rate swaps not designated as hedges are reported in other income, net. In October 2022, the Company entered into interest rate swap contracts with a total notional amount of $1.25 billion, paying a weighted-average fixed rate of 4.53% and receiving a variable rate based on compound overnight SOFR from November 2022 through June 2023, settled monthly. In March 2023, the Company entered into swaps with a total notional amount of $1.2 billion, paying a weighted-average fixed rate of 3.88% and receiving a variable rate based on 1-month Term SOFR from July 2023 through June 2024, settled monthly. As of June 30, 2023, the Company had no other receive-variable/pay-fixed interest rate swaps beyond those listed, and as of June 30, 2022, it had no such swaps. Although hedge accounting is not applied, the Company believes these economic hedges are effective in protecting against changes in variable interest rates on forecasted commercial paper issuances. As of June 30, 2023 and 2022, the total notional amount of receive-fixed/pay-variable interest rate swaps was $650 million. To manage foreign currency risk, the Company uses forward contracts, with qualifying contracts designated as cash flow hedges of forecasted transactions in foreign currencies. The effective portion of changes in fair value is reported in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) and reclassified into earnings in the same line item and period as the related hedged transaction. The ineffective portion is recognized in earnings in the same line item as the underlying hedged item. Changes in fair value of forward contracts not designated as hedges are reported in other income, net. As of June 30, 2023 and 2022, the notional amount of outstanding forward contracts was $0.5 billion and $1.0 billion, respectively. To manage commodity price risk, the Company passes through price volatility to customers, including through fixed price swaps. In some cases, the Company purchases fixed price commodity swaps on behalf of customers to offset price volatility on underlying sales contracts, which are cash closed out at maturity and the related cost or benefit is passed through to customers. Commodity price exposure is derived from customer supply forecasts and hedged by central treasury units. Changes in the fair value of commodity hedges are recognized in AOCI and the cumulative amount is recognized in the consolidated statements of income when the forecasted transaction is realized. ## 🔍 What-If Scenario Mapping: Article 6 – Elective Deferrals

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 1:
> *"An Employee who was not otherwise eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits for a Plan Year and first satisfies the requirements for participation during one of the first three quarters of the Plan Year by reason of exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limit will become eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits under the Plan effective January 1 of the following Plan Year..."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if a new employee exceeds the Section 401(a)(17) limit in Q2 of the 2024 Plan Year?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
The employee becomes eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits **effective January 1, 2025** (the next Plan Year).  
They can participate in the **open enrollment period** for 2025, but **not** in a mid-year election.  
Their Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date is **January 1, 2025**.

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This shows that **exceeding the 401(a)(17) limit early in the year** (Q1–Q3) triggers a **delayed eligibility** — not immediate. The rule is designed to prevent "gaming" the system by timing compensation to hit the limit just before the end of the year.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 2:
> *"An Employee who first satisfies the requirements for participation during the final calendar quarter of the Plan Year by reason of exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limit will become eligible... as of the first pay period beginning after the first day of the second month of the first calendar quarter of the following Plan Year."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if a mid-level employee exceeds the 401(a)(17) limit in Q4 of 2024 (e.g., due to a bonus spike)?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
The employee becomes eligible **as of the first pay period after February 1, 2025** (i.e., the first pay period in Q1 of 2025).  
They can make a **mid-year election** (if permitted under Section 6.2(b)(ii)) **before** that date, up to the deadline set by the Administrator.

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This is a **critical exception** — it allows for **faster eligibility** when the limit is exceeded in the final quarter. It gives employees a chance to plan for deferrals earlier than January 1.  
This also shows that **timing of the exceedance** changes the eligibility date — a key conditional logic point.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 3:
> *"Mid-year elections are not allowed... unless the Employee also satisfies all the requirements of Section 6.3..."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if a new employee exceeds the 401(a)(17) limit in Q3 and wants to make a mid-year deferral election?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
❌ **The mid-year election is NOT allowed**.  
Even though they became eligible due to exceeding the limit, they **do not qualify** for mid-year enrollment under Section 6.2(b)(ii) because **they did not satisfy the Section 6.3 conditions** (specifically, they must have previously been eligible for an elective account-balance plan or meet the "newly eligible" criteria).

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This highlights a **common misconception**: just becoming eligible due to a 401(a)(17) exceedance does **not** automatically grant mid-year election rights.  
Only employees who meet **Section 6.3(a) or (b)** — such as those who previously participated in deferred plans and then lost eligibility — can make mid-year elections.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 4:
> *"An Employee who had previously been eligible to participate in an elective account-balance deferred compensation arrangement... may be treated as newly eligible to participate and entitled to mid-year enrollment..."*
