> **What if a former employee who previously deferred under Amex’s plan (and had no deferrals left) returns to work in Q3 2024 and exceeds the 401(a)(17) limit?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
✅ The employee **is treated as newly eligible** under Section 6.3.  
They **can make a mid-year deferral election** before the deadline established by the Administrator (e.g., in Q4 2024).  
Their Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date is set as the **first payroll period after the expiration of the 30-day window** from the date they first became eligible (i.e., after the exceedance).

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This shows that **prior participation history** can override the standard "January 1" rule. It creates a **pathway for continuity** for employees returning after a break — a key feature for retention and flexibility.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 5:
> *"The Administrator may impose further limits on the amount or percentage that can be deferred from Base Salary and/or Incentive Pay for a given Plan Year."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if the Administrator decides to cap Incentive Pay deferrals at 70% instead of the default 85%?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
All employees who make a deferral election will now be limited to **70% of their Incentive Pay** (instead of 85%).  
This limit applies **only to the second following Plan Year** (or the following year in mid-year cases).  
The cap is **imposed no later than the day before the election takes effect**.

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This demonstrates **administrative discretion** — the plan can adjust deferral limits based on financial or regulatory considerations.  
It also shows that such changes are **effective retroactively** to future elections, not past ones.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 6:
> *"A Participant who has not previously modified an initial Supplemental Election may make a one-time modification... provided it complies with Section 409A (including a 5-year deferral and 12-month waiting period)."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if a participant who rehired after separation wants to change their payment method from annual installments to a lump sum?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
✅ The participant **can make a one-time modification** under Section 5.4(d), **but only for benefits earned after rehire**.  
The change must:  
- Be filed in writing by the Administrator’s prescribed form,  
- Comply with Section 409A (minimum 5-year deferral, effective 12 months after filing),  
- Be effective only for **post-rehire benefits**, not pre-separation benefits.

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This shows that **rehire rules are not symmetric** — they apply only to **newly earned benefits**, not to past ones. It protects the integrity of pre-existing benefit obligations.

---

### 📌 Conditional Clause 7:
> *"Participants who have previously made both a Supplemental Election and a modification to such Supplemental Election shall be subject to the rules of Section 5.4(d) prohibiting any further changes."*

#### ✅ What-If Scenario:
> **What if a participant made a Supplemental Election in 2020 and later modified it in 2022, and now wants to change it again in 2025?**

➡️ **Outcome**:  
❌ **No further modifications are allowed**.  
They are **locked in** under Section 5.4(d) — even if they want to switch from lump sum to installments or vice versa.

🔹 *Why this matters*:  
This enforces **stability in benefit structures** — once a participant has modified their election, they cannot "game" the system by changing it again. It prevents administrative chaos and ensures predictability.

---

## ✅ Summary Table: Key What-If Outcomes

| Scenario | Outcome | Key Conditional Trigger |
|--------|--------|------------------------|
| Exceeds 401(a)(17) in Q1–Q3 | Eligible Jan 1 next year | Timing of exceedance |
| Exceeds 401(a)(17) in Q4 | Eligible in Feb–Mar next year | Final quarter exceedance |
| New hire exceeds limit in Q3 wants mid-year election | ❌ Not allowed | No Section 6.3 eligibility |
| Former employee returns, had prior deferrals | ✅ Can make mid-year election | Section 6.3(a) or (b) |
| Admin lowers Incentive Pay cap | New limit applies to future elections | Admin discretion |
| Rehired employee wants to modify election | ✅ Allowed only for post-rehire benefits | Rehire date = new eligibility |
| Participant modified election twice | ❌ No further changes | Section 5.4(d) lock-in |

---

## 🎯 Learning Takeaways

1. **Timing matters**: The **quarter** in which a 401(a)(17) limit is exceeded determines eligibility date — not just whether it's exceeded.
2. **Mid-year elections are conditional**: They only apply to employees who meet **Section 6.3** criteria — not just those who become eligible via a limit exceedance.
3. **Past participation history unlocks flexibility**: Employees with prior deferred plan experience can re-enter with mid-year options.
4. **Administrative discretion is real**: Limits can be changed, but only before elections take effect.
5. **Rehires are treated as new starts**: Benefits earned after rehire are subject to new election rules — not old ones.
6. **Once modified, elections are locked**: Prevents over-modification and ensures stability.

---

## 💡 Final Tip for Future Use

When reading complex benefit plans, **always ask**:  
> *"What if this rule applies in a realistic, edge-case scenario?"*  

This forces you to **test the logic**, not just memorize the text. It turns passive reading into active engagement — and builds **intuitive understanding** of how the plan actually works in real life.

---

text: Assets impaired as a result of the Company’s restructuring efforts are written down to their fair value less costs to sell when the Company commits to disposing of them and they are no longer in use. Depreciation is accelerated on fixed assets during the period the asset is in use until it ceases to be used. Other restructuring costs, such as those for relocating equipment, are recorded as they are incurred or when services are provided. See Note 7, "Restructuring," for further details on the Company’s restructuring plans. Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash are defined as highly liquid investments with a maturity of three months or less when purchased. Cash equivalents include demand deposits that can be readily liquidated without penalty and are carried at cost, which approximates fair market value. As of June 30, 2022, the Company had restricted cash of $8 million held in a share trust related to share-based payment obligations; this amount was immaterial as of June 30, 2023. Trade receivables, net of allowance for credit losses, are recorded at the amount expected to be collected, net of an allowance for sales returns and estimated losses due to customers’ inability to pay. The allowance for doubtful accounts is estimated using the current expected credit loss model (CECL), incorporating past events, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts of future economic conditions. Factors considered in evaluating specific customer accounts include creditworthiness, past transaction history, and changes in payment terms or practices. Overall historical collection experience, current industry trends, and a review of trade receivables are also considered. Changes in the allowance for doubtful accounts were not material for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2023, 2022, and 2021. The Company occasionally enters into customer-based supply-chain financing programs to sell trade receivables to third-party financial institutions. Agreements that result in true sales—defined as transfers without recourse—are reflected as a reduction of trade receivables, net on the consolidated balance sheets, and the proceeds are included in cash flows from operating activities. Agreements that allow the Company to maintain effective control over the receivables and do not qualify as true sales are accounted for as secured borrowings and recorded within trade receivables, net and short-term debt. Expenses related to receivables factoring are recorded primarily as a reduction of net sales. The Company did not factor any trade receivables in fiscal years 2023 and 2022 that did not qualify as true sales. Inventories are stated at the lower of cost and net realizable value, with cost based on the first-in, first-out (FIFO) or average cost method. Costs include raw materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. Inventory reserves were $130 million and $111 million as of June 30, 2023 and 2022, respectively. Property, plant, and equipment, net (PP&E), is carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment and includes expenditures for new facilities and equipment, as well as costs that substantially increase the useful lives or capacity of existing PP&E. Capitalized interest during construction is included in the cost of constructed assets. Maintenance and repairs that do not improve efficiency or extend economic life are expensed as incurred. PP&E, including assets held under finance leases, is depreciated using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets or, for leasehold improvements and finance leases, over the lease term or useful life of the asset. The Company periodically reviews these useful lives and makes prospective changes when appropriate. Leasehold land is depreciated over the lease term; land improvements over up to 30 years; buildings over up to 45 years; machinery and equipment over up to 25 years; and finance leases over the lease term or 5 to 25 years. Long-lived assets, primarily PP&E and certain identifiable intangible assets with finite lives, are reviewed for impairment when facts or circumstances indicate the carrying amount may not be recoverable. If estimated future undiscounted cash flows are less than carrying value, the carrying value is reduced to fair value, determined using quoted market values, discounted cash flows, or external appraisals. Impairment losses recognized in the consolidated statements of income, excluding assets held for sale, were $18 million in 2023, $43 million in 2022, and $10 million in 2021. For leases with original terms exceeding twelve months, the Company recognizes a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability. Short-term leases of twelve months or less are not recorded on the balance sheets, and lease expenses are recognized on a straight-line basis. Lease liabilities are recognized at the commencement date based on the present value of remaining lease payments, including noncancellable terms and renewal periods the Company is reasonably certain to exercise. A significant portion of the Company’s leases includes options to extend, and the Company regularly re-evaluates these options based on economic and strategic incentives. Since implicit rates in leases are generally not readily determinable, the Company uses its estimated incremental borrowing rate as the discount rate. Variable lease payments dependent on usage, output, or other factors are excluded from lease payments in measuring the ROU asset and lease liability and are recognized as expenses in the period the obligation arises. Goodwill represents the excess of cost over the fair value of net assets acquired in business combinations and is not amortized but is tested annually for impairment in the fourth quarter or when events or circumstances indicate impairment may have occurred. The Company has six reporting units with goodwill, each assessed for impairment. The Company may first perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative assessment is necessary; if the qualitative assessment indicates it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value, a quantitative assessment is performed using a discounted cash flow model. Key assumptions in the model include revenue growth, projected operating income growth, market multiples, terminal values, and discount rates. Sensitivity analyses are performed to assess the reasonableness of assumptions and resulting fair values. If future growth rates or margins do not meet expectations or if market factors beyond the Company’s control, such as changes in discount rates or economic or political conditions in key markets, significantly change, goodwill may be impaired. In fiscal year 2023, the Company performed quantitative impairment tests for all reporting units and concluded that goodwill was not impaired because the fair values substantially exceeded carrying values. Contractual or separable intangible assets with finite useful lives are amortized on a straight-line basis over their estimated useful lives, ranging from 1 to 20 years. Costs to develop software for internal use are capitalized as computer software within other intangible assets. Fair value measurements reflect the amounts that would be received to sell assets or paid to transfer liabilities in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date (exit price). The Company uses a three-tiered fair value hierarchy: Level 1 includes quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities; Level 2 uses directly or indirectly observable inputs; Level 3 uses unobservable inputs, such as internally developed pricing models. Derivative instruments are recognized at fair value on the consolidated balance sheets. Gains or losses from derivatives not designated as hedges are recognized in income. For hedging instruments, changes in fair value are either offset against changes in the fair value of the hedged items through earnings or recognized in shareholders’ equity through other comprehensive income/(loss) until the hedged item is recognized. Ineffective portions of hedges are recognized in earnings over the life of the hedging relationship. See Note 12, "Derivative Instruments," for details on forward foreign currency exchange contracts, currency swap contracts, and interest rate swap arrangements. The Company sponsors defined contribution plans, with expenses of $87 million, $79 million, and $68 million for fiscal years ended June 30, 2023, 2022, and 2021, respectively. The Company also sponsors defined benefit plans, requiring management to make assumptions about the long-term rate of return on plan assets, discount rates, salary inflation, mortality rates, and other factors. These assumptions are considered critical accounting estimates due to their sensitivity to changes in plan asset performance, actuarial valuations, market conditions, and contracted benefits. Assumptions are based on historical trends, known economic and market conditions, and independent actuarial studies. Actual results may differ significantly from estimates. The funded status of each defined benefit pension plan is recognized in the consolidated balance sheets: overfunded plans are recorded as assets in employee benefit assets, underfunded plans as liabilities in employee benefit obligations. Pension plan liabilities are revalued annually or when an event requires remeasurement based on updated assumptions and information about plan participants. Accumulated actuarial gains and losses in excess of a 10 percent corridor and prior service cost are amortized on a straight-line basis over the average remaining service period of active participants or the average life expectancy for plans with significant inactive participants. Service costs are included in operating income; other components of net benefit cost are recorded in other non-operating income, net. Investments in companies where the Company exercises significant influence over operating and financial policies are accounted for under the equity method. Investments in limited partnerships or limited liability companies with separate ownership accounts are also accounted for under the equity method unless the Company’s interest is minor and has no influence. Under this method, the investment is carried at cost and adjusted to reflect the investor’s share of earnings or losses after acquisition, and is impaired if a decline in fair value below cost is other than temporary. The fair value becomes the new cost basis and is not adjusted for subsequent recoveries. The Company reviews equity method investments for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying amount may not be recoverable. All equity investments not consolidated and not accounted for under the equity method are measured at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses included in net income. For investments without readily determinable fair values, the Company uses the measurement alternative, measuring them at cost adjusted for impairments and observable price changes in orderly transactions. See Note 8, "Equity Method and Other Investments," for more information. The Company is subject to various contingencies, including legal and administrative proceedings, environmental claims, workers’ compensation, and other claims. Accruals for estimated losses are recorded when information indicates losses are probable and reasonably estimable. If a range of losses is reasonably estimable, the best estimate within the range is accrued; if no amount in the range is a better estimate, the low end is accrued. Anticipated recoveries under existing insurance contracts are recorded when recovery is probable. Share-based compensation includes various equity incentive plans. For awards with service or market conditions, compensation expense is recognized over the vesting period on a straight-line basis using the grant date fair value and the estimated number of awards expected to vest. For performance-based awards, the Company reassesses the probability of vesting at each reporting period and adjusts compensation cost accordingly. Immaterial cash-settled share-based compensation plans are accounted for as liabilities and are remeasured to fair value at each reporting date. The Company estimates forfeitures based on employee level, time remaining to vest, and historical forfeiture experience. The Company uses the asset and liability method for income taxes. Deferred income taxes reflect future tax consequences of temporary differences between the tax bases of assets and liabilities and their financial reporting amounts, based on enacted tax laws and rates. Income tax expense or benefit is based on earnings reported in the consolidated financial statements. The provision differs from current tax payable due to timing differences in income and expense recognition by taxing authorities. Deferred tax assets, including operating losses, capital losses, and tax credit carryforwards, are reduced by a valuation allowance when it is more likely than not that any portion will not be realized. Management periodically assesses the need to accrue or disclose uncertain tax positions, analyzing complex tax laws across multiple jurisdictions. Accounting guidance requires a recognition threshold and measurement attribute for tax positions. Related interest expense and penalties, if any, are recorded as tax expense. See Note 17, "Income Taxes," for more information. In November 2021, the FASB issued ASU 2021-10, Government Assistance, (Topic 832), which adds disclosure requirements for entities receiving government assistance. The standard is effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2021, with early adoption permitted. The Company adopted ASU 2021-10 on July 1, 2022. The Company analyzed government assistance received and determined that the amounts, both individually and in the aggregate, are not material. ASU 2021-10 may impact future disclosures if government assistance becomes material. In September 2022, the FASB issued ASU 2022-04, which adds disclosure requirements for entities that use supplier finance programs in connection with purchases.

record of the Notes to be redeemed at its registered address, at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount thereof plus accrued interest to the date fixed for redemption; provided, ### **Data Limitations Section (Applied Learning Strategy)**  
*Focus: Identifying data gaps and their implications for risk assessment*

The document contains significant **data limitations**, particularly for **corporate card member loans and receivables**, which directly impact the accuracy and completeness of risk assessments. Below is a dedicated "Data Limitations" section that flags each missing or restricted metric and clearly explains its **implication for risk evaluation**.

---

#### 🔍 **Data Limitations and Their Implications for Risk Assessment**

| Missing/Restricted Metric | Why It’s Missing | Impact on Risk Assessment |
|--------------------------|------------------|----------------------------|
| **Delinquency data for 30–89 days past due (corporate accounts)** | Delinquency data for periods other than 90+ days past billing is not available due to system constraints. | ❌ Cannot assess early delinquency trends or identify emerging risk in corporate accounts before they reach 90 days past billing. This creates a **critical blind spot** in monitoring credit deterioration. Risk managers cannot detect or respond to early warning signs of financial distress. |
| **Net write-off rate for corporate loans (principal only)** | Net write-off rate based on principal losses is not available due to system constraints. | ❌ Risk exposure is **not fully quantified**. Without this key metric, the organization cannot measure the proportion of corporate loans that are ultimately written off, making it impossible to evaluate loss severity or model expected credit losses (ECL) accurately. This undermines the CECL methodology’s reliance on historical loss experience. |
| **Net write-off rate for corporate receivables (principal only)** | Same as above — data not available due to system constraints. | ❌ Corporate receivables are treated differently from consumer and small business segments, yet lack key credit quality indicators. This leads to **inconsistent risk modeling** across customer types and may result in underestimating losses in corporate receivables. |
| **Delinquency data for 30–89 days past due (corporate receivables)** | System constraints prevent tracking delinquency below 90 days past billing. | ❌ No visibility into early-stage delinquency in corporate receivables. This limits the ability to assess collection trends, predict defaults, or adjust provisioning policies in a timely manner. |
| **Interest and fees component in net write-off rate (corporate)** | While interest and fees are included in total provision, the breakdown is not available for corporate accounts. | ⚠️ Risk assessment is incomplete because the full cost of non-recovery (including interest and fees) is not captured. This affects the accuracy of total credit loss estimates and may lead to **under-provisioning** if only principal is considered. |
| **TDRs (Troubled Debt Restructurings) for corporate accounts** | Corporate accounts are not included in TDR classifications. | ❌ Corporate customers are excluded from TDR programs and related risk disclosures. This means **no visibility into financial relief efforts**, potential default risks from modifications, or recovery outcomes for corporate clients. Risk models may miss a major source of future losses. |
| **Default rates within 12 months of TDR modification (corporate)** | No data on corporate TDRs that subsequently defaulted. | ❌ Cannot evaluate the effectiveness of TDR programs for corporate clients. Without this, the organization cannot determine whether modifications are reducing or increasing risk — a key input for future policy decisions. |

---

### 📌 Key Takeaways from Data Limitations

1. **Corporate segment is effectively "invisible" in early-stage delinquency tracking**  
   - All delinquency data is only available at the 90+ days past billing threshold.  
   - This means **early risk signals are missed**, and risk deterioration goes undetected until late stages.

2. **Critical credit quality metrics are missing**  
   - Net write-off rates (principal only) are unavailable — a foundational metric for loss modeling under CECL.  
   - Without these, the company cannot apply consistent risk weights or validate its reserve assumptions for corporate portfolios.

3. **TDR programs are not monitored for corporate clients**  
   - The absence of TDR data means corporate customers are not being actively managed during financial stress.  
   - This increases exposure to unexpected defaults and reduces the ability to mitigate losses through structured relief.

4. **Risk assessment is inherently biased toward consumer and small business segments**  
   - The data structure reflects a **segmental bias** where corporate accounts are treated as a "black box" with limited transparency.  
   - This could lead to **over-reliance on historical trends from other segments**, which may not be applicable to corporate clients.

---

### ✅ Recommendations Based on Data Gaps

- **Prioritize system upgrades** to enable delinquency tracking for corporate accounts below 90 days past due.  
- **Develop alternative risk indicators** (e.g., payment history, spend patterns, external financial data) to proxy for early delinquency in corporate accounts.  
- **Conduct sensitivity analysis** on reserve estimates assuming different levels of corporate delinquency and write-offs to understand the impact of missing data.  
- **Include corporate accounts in TDR monitoring** and track default outcomes post-modification to improve risk modeling.  
- **Disclose data limitations transparently** in risk reports to stakeholders, ensuring informed decision-making.

---

### Final Note  
> **"Missing data is not neutral — it distorts risk perception and leads to flawed decisions."**  
This document reveals that while the company has robust risk frameworks for consumer and small business segments, **corporate accounts are systematically excluded from key risk monitoring and modeling processes**. This gap must be addressed to ensure a comprehensive, fair, and accurate risk assessment across all customer types.

---  
✅ *Strategy applied: Focus on identifying data gaps and their implications for risk assessment.*

text: The Issuer and the Guarantors have existing commercial deposits and custodial arrangements with Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas ("Deutsche Bank") and may have borrowed money from Deutsche Bank or its affiliates in the ordinary course of business; they may also enter into similar or other banking relationships with Deutsche Bank or its affiliates in the future. Deutsche Bank may serve as trustee for other debt securities issued by the Issuer and the Guarantors. Neither the Issuer nor any Guarantor is required to make sinking fund payments or offers to purchase the Notes or the Guarantees, although the Issuer or Guarantors may at any time purchase Notes in the open market or otherwise. Under the indenture, the Issuer and each Guarantor have agreed to the following covenants: upon a Change of Control Triggering Event, unless the Issuer redeems the Notes in accordance with their terms, each holder may require the Issuer to repurchase all or part of their Notes at 101% of the principal amount plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, up to the purchase date, subject to holders' rights to receive interest due on the relevant interest payment date. Within 30 days after the Change of Control Triggering Event occurs—or at the Issuer’s option, prior to the Change of Control but after public announcement—the Issuer must send by first-class mail a notice to each holder of the Notes, with a copy to the Trustee, governing the Change of Control Offer. The notice must specify the purchase date, which must be no earlier than 30 days and no later than 60 days from the mailing date (except as required by law), and if mailed before the Change of Control is consummated, it must state that the offer is conditional on the Change of Control being completed on or before the Change of Control Payment Date. Holders electing to have their Notes purchased must surrender the Notes, with the "Option of Holder to Elect Purchase" form completed, to the Trustee at the address in the notice or transfer them by book-entry transfer prior to the close of business on the third Business Day before the Change of Control Payment Date. The Issuer is not required to make a Change of Control Offer if a third party makes such an offer in the same manner, at the same times, and otherwise in compliance with the requirements, and purchases all properly tendered and not withdrawn Notes. A Change of Control includes a direct or indirect sale, lease, transfer, conveyance, or other disposition of "all or substantially all" of the Issuer’s and its subsidiaries’ assets taken as a whole. Although there is limited case law on "substantially all," there is no established legal definition, so the applicability of the repurchase requirement for a disposition of less than all assets to another "person" (as defined in Section 13(d)(3) of the Exchange Act) is uncertain. The indenture restricts the creation of liens on any present or future assets of Amcor or its subsidiaries to secure Indebtedness, unless the Notes and applicable Guarantees are secured equally and ratably (or prior) to such Indebtedness, with exceptions including: (a) liens on assets securing Indebtedness outstanding on the date of the indenture; (b) liens on assets securing Indebtedness owed to Amcor or a Subsidiary (other than a Project Subsidiary); (c) existing liens on assets prior to acquisition, provided they were not created in anticipation of acquisition, do not extend to other assets (except proceeds, products, or after-acquired property affixed or incorporated into the asset), secure only the Indebtedness in place at acquisition, and are discharged within one year or by maturity of the secured debt if fixed-rate and commercially advantageous; (d) liens on assets of a Person that becomes a Subsidiary or is merged into a Subsidiary after the original issue date, with similar conditions; (e) liens for Indebtedness incurred to purchase Equity Interests or other assets (excluding real or personal property under clause (f)), securing only such Indebtedness, applying only to the purchased assets and proceeds, and being discharged within two years; (f) liens for Indebtedness to acquire or develop real or personal property, securing only such Indebtedness, not extending to other assets (except proceeds, products, or after-acquired property affixed or incorporated), and limiting the holder’s recourse to the property subject to the lien; (g) liens for borrowings from financial institutions to finance import or export contracts where part of the price is guaranteed or insured, applying only to the related assets and not exceeding the amount guaranteed or insured; (h) liens from international or governmental development agencies for specific projects, required by law or practice and limited to assets used in or derived from the project; (i) liens created with co-venturers in unincorporated joint ventures, securing only obligations under the agreement and applying only to the joint venture’s Equity Interests or assets; (j) liens on goods or documents of title arising in the ordinary course of business in connection with letters of credit, securing only the acquisition cost or selling price (and incidental amounts) payable within 180 days; (k) liens arising by operation of law in the ordinary course of business; (l) liens over Project Assets, securing only Limited Recourse Indebtedness as defined; (m) liens arising under netting or set-off arrangements in the ordinary course of banking; (n) refinancing of liens permitted under clauses (a) through (m), provided the refinanced lien does not extend to assets not previously covered, the principal amount does not exceed the original secured amount, and for refinancings under (c) through (e), the original discharge timelines remain unchanged; (o) liens arising from a Change in Lease Accounting Standard; and (p) other liens, provided that immediately after incurrence or assumption, the aggregate principal amount of all Indebtedness secured by such liens does not exceed 10% of Total Tangible Assets. There are no restrictions on the amount of unsecured Indebtedness that Amcor or its subsidiaries may have outstanding. The indenture also prohibits the Issuer or any applicable Guarantor from consolidating with or merging into a Person that is not the Issuer or a Guarantor, or conveying, transferring, or leasing all or substantially all of its properties and assets to a Person not the Issuer or a Guarantor, unless: (1) the resulting entity is a corporation, partnership, or trust organized and validly existing under the laws of the United States, a U.S. state, the District of Columbia, Jersey, the Commonwealth of Australia, the United Kingdom, or a state or territory thereof, and either is the Issuer or an applicable Guarantor or assumes the obligations of the Notes or Guarantees via a supplemental indenture, including obligations to pay Additional Amounts; (2) immediately after the transaction, no Event of Default exists or would result after notice or lapse of time; (3) if the entity is not incorporated under U.S. or applicable foreign law, it must expressly agree in a supplemental indenture to indemnify holders and beneficial owners against taxes, duties, assessments, or governmental charges arising from the transaction and to make payments on the Notes or Guarantees without withholding for taxes imposed by the jurisdiction of organization or residency, unless required by law, in which case it will pay additional amounts ("Successor Additional Amounts") to ensure holders receive the same amounts as if no withholding occurred, subject to the same exceptions as apply to the original Issuer or Guarantor; and (4) certain other conditions are met. These provisions do not necessarily protect Note holders in highly leveraged or other transactions that may adversely affect the Notes. The Issuer may make changes to the indenture or Notes in three ways: changes requiring unanimous consent of holders of affected Notes include: changing the stated maturity, any installment of principal, premium (if any), or interest, or the interest rate, or altering the Issuer’s obligation to pay Additional Amounts; changing the place or currency of payment; impairing any holder’s ability to sue for payment; reducing the principal payable upon acceleration following an Event of Default; reducing any amounts due on the Notes; reducing the aggregate principal amount of Notes requiring holder consent to modify or amend the indenture; reducing the aggregate principal amount of Notes requiring holder consent to waive compliance with certain indenture provisions or certain defaults; modifying any aspect of the modification or waiver provisions in a way that adversely affects holders; or modifying the terms and conditions of the applicable Guarantors’ payment obligations (including Additional Amounts) in a way that adversely affects holders.

text: Our funding structure relies on bank overdrafts, bank loans, corporate bonds, unsecured notes, and commercial paper. To manage liquidity risk, we maintain a minimum undrawn committed liquidity of at least $200 million that can be drawn at short notice; conduct regular comprehensive analyses of cash inflows and outflows related to operational, investing, and financing activities; use only tradable instruments in highly liquid markets; maintain a senior credit investment grade rating with a reputable independent rating agency; manage credit risk associated with financial assets; monitor the duration of long-term debt; invest surplus cash only with major financial institutions or well-diversified money market funds; and, where practicable, spread the maturity dates of long-term debt facilities. Our three- and five-year syndicated facility agreements each provide a revolving credit facility of $1.9 billion, totaling $3.8 billion. These facilities are unsecured and have contractual maturities in April 2025 and April 2027, respectively, with two 12-month extension options available for each tranche. As of June 30, 2023 and 2022, $2.5 billion and $2.4 billion, respectively, were drawn under commercial paper programs, which are backstopped by committed bank syndicated loan facilities maturing in April 2025 ($1.9 billion) and April 2027 ($1.9 billion), with $1.3 billion in unused capacity remaining as of June 30, 2023. We expect future long-term funding needs to primarily involve refinancing and servicing maturing financial liabilities as outlined above, as well as financing capital expenditures and potential acquisitions. We will continue to fund long-term business needs through operating cash flow and the management of business capital, particularly via regular issuances of commercial paper and debt securities. Discretionary growth capital expenditures and acquisitions are evaluated individually based on return on investment after financing costs, payback period, and mid-term liquidity planning covering four years post the current fiscal year. Our long-term liquidity access depends on both operational results and market availability of funding. The preparation of our consolidated financial statements under U.S. GAAP requires estimates and assumptions affecting asset and liability reporting and expense recognition, including those related to retirement benefits, intangible assets, goodwill, and future operational performance. These estimates are based on historical experience and other factors considered reasonable at the time. Actual results may differ from these estimates. Critical accounting estimates include pensions, goodwill and intangible assets, deferred taxes, and uncertain tax positions. Most defined benefit pension plans are closed to new entrants and future accruals; net periodic pension costs were $11 million in fiscal year 2023, $12 million in 2022, and $15 million in 2021, with an expected $11 million for fiscal year 2024 before income taxes. Assumptions such as long-term rate of return on plan assets, discount rates, salary inflation, mortality rates, and other factors are based on historical trends, known market conditions, and independent actuarial studies. The difference between plan asset fair value and projected benefit obligation is recorded as an asset or liability on the balance sheet. Gains or losses and prior service costs are recorded in other comprehensive income/(loss). Pension liabilities are revalued annually or when events require remeasurement, using updated assumptions and participant data. Accumulated actuarial gains or losses exceeding a 10% corridor and prior service costs are amortized over the average remaining service period of active participants or average life expectancy for inactive participants. Discount rates are determined using a high-quality corporate bond yield curve from reputable third-party sources, or a government bond approach in markets with limited corporate bond depth. Expected long-term rates of return are derived from individual asset class assumptions and combined into a single plan-level assumption based on target asset allocation. A sensitivity analysis shows that a 25 basis point increase in the discount rate or a 25 basis point decrease in the expected return on plan assets would impact pension expense by $1 million and $3 million, respectively. Goodwill, representing the excess of purchase price over fair value of net assets, is not amortized but tested annually in the fourth quarter or when impairment indicators arise. We have six reporting units, five of which are in the Flexibles segment, and one in the Rigid Packaging segment. Impairment assessments may begin with a qualitative review; if a quantitative test is needed, fair values are estimated using income approaches, relying on assumptions such as revenue growth, operating income growth, market multiples, terminal values, and discount rates. When a reporting unit’s carrying value exceeds its fair value, an impairment loss is recognized, limited to goodwill carrying value and adjusted for tax benefits. These goodwill impairment estimates are critical due to the significant amount of goodwill and the judgment required in determining fair value and projected cash flows. Factors such as declining net earnings, adverse equity market conditions, or rising interest rates may trigger more frequent assessments. Intangible assets, including customer relationships, technology, trademarks, and software, are amortized straight-line over useful lives ranging from one to twenty years and are reviewed for impairment when events suggest unrecoverable value. Impairment testing requires estimates of fair value based on projected future cash flows and discount rates, involving judgments about future events and cash flows. Deferred tax assets and uncertain tax positions require significant judgment due to the complexity of tax laws and differing interpretations. Determining uncertain tax positions involves evaluating whether it is more likely than not that a position will be sustained upon audit, including appeals or litigation. Recognized tax benefits are measured as the largest benefit of a more likely than not likelihood of being sustained. We assess the recoverability of deferred tax assets against future taxable income, which may require a valuation allowance, especially for operating losses, capital losses, and tax credits. Factors considered include expected future performance, timing of temporary difference reversals, and tax planning feasibility. Changes in tax laws or statutory rates could require adjustments to valuation allowances or deferred tax liabilities, impacting financial position and results. Disposal groups held for sale are assessed for impairment by comparing fair value less cost to sell to carrying value, using valuation techniques such as earnings multiples, discounted cash flows, and indicative bids. Significant estimates include sales, expenses, and other factors, derived from historical experience, third-party guidance, and available information. The actual realization of fair value upon divestiture may differ significantly, especially for disposal groups in conflict regions. We have no material changes in market risks for fiscal years 2023 and 2022, except for increased volatility due to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the COVID-19 pandemic. Interest rate risk is managed through a mix of fixed and variable-rate debt, monitoring global rates, and using interest rate derivatives such as swaps and locks. A 1% increase in the floating rate on U.S. dollar and Euro-denominated instruments as of June 30, 2023, would result in a $20 million adverse impact on income before income taxes and equity in income. Foreign exchange risk arises from operations in over 40 countries; a 1% adverse change in the average Euro exchange rate would reduce net sales by $26 million. In fiscal year 2023, 52% of net sales were effectively generated in U.S. dollar functional currency entities, 18% in Euro entities, and the remaining 30% in other functional currencies. The translation of Euro and other non-U.S. dollar sales and expenses into U.S. dollars varies with currency movements. Raw material and commodity price risk stems from resins, film, chemicals, and aluminum; a 1% increase in average prices not passed on to customers would increase cost of sales and reduce income before income taxes by $67 million. Credit risk arises from financing activities, including bank deposits, foreign exchange transactions, and derivative instruments. ### 🔹 Edge Case 1: *Participant dies 3 months after retirement eligibility is reached, but before any payments begin*

> **What if?** A participant elected installments to be paid on January 1/July 1. They become disabled 4 months before the first payment date. The disability starts on June 1, 2024. The first payment would have been July 1, 2024.

- Disability occurs on **June 1, 2024**.

From the document, the following **parallel regulatory frameworks** stand out:

| Framework | Key Features |
|--------|-------------|
| **Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA)** | Resolution regime under FDIC/Treasury; used for systemically important institutions; allows FDIC to disregard claim priorities, use administrative claims procedures, transfer claims to bridge entities |
| **U.S. Bankruptcy Code** | Judicial process for insolvency; strict creditor claim priority rules; judicial determination of claims; limited ability to repudiate obligations |
| **FDIC Resolution Plans (for large institutions)** | Pre-emptive resolution planning; 3-year cycle; required for institutions with $100B+ assets (like AENB) |
| **Deposit Insurance & FDIA** | FDIC insures deposits up to limits; can terminate insurance if unsafe/unsound practices are found |
| **CRA (Community Reinvestment Act)** | Affirmative obligation to serve local communities; ongoing compliance |
| **Climate Risk Principles (OCC, FDIC, Fed)** | Guidance for large banks on climate risk management; not binding but influential |
| **Consumer Financial Protection (CFPB)** | Regulates credit, lending, fees; enforces "unfair, deceptive, abusive" practices |
| **Interchange Fee Regulations (EU, Australia, Canada)** | Caps on fees paid by merchants to card issuers; affects revenue and business model |

| **AML/CFT (U.S. Patriot Act, EU Directives)** | Global compliance; U.S. has centralized reporting; EU has decentralized implementation |

## 📊 Step 2: Apply Contrast Mapping – Side-by-Side Comparison Table

We now create a **contrast mapping table** focusing on **the most functionally distinct pairs**:

---

### ✅ Contrast 1: **OLA vs. U.S. Bankruptcy Code**  
*(Resolution of Financial Institution Failure)*

| Feature | **Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA)** | **U.S. Bankruptcy Code** | **Contrast** |
|--------|----------------------------------------|--------------------------|-------------|
| **Governing Body** | FDIC as receiver (appointed by Treasury) | Bankruptcy Court (judicial process) | OLA is **administrative**, not judicial |
| **Claim Priority** | FDIC may **disregard strict priority** of creditor claims in limited circumstances | Strict **priority hierarchy** (e.g., deposits > unsecured creditors) | OLA allows **flexibility**; Bankruptcy enforces **rigid order** |
| **Claims Determination** | Uses **administrative claims procedure** (FDIC-led) | Uses **judicial claims process** (court review) | OLA is **faster, less adversarial**; Bankruptcy is **more formal and contested** |
| **Transfer of Claims** | FDIC can **transfer claims to a “bridge” entity** | Claims remain with debtor; no such transfer | OLA enables **restructuring via bridge company**; Bankruptcy does not |
| **Contract Repudiation** | FDIC may **repudiate or disaffirm** contracts deemed burdensome | Repudiation is **rare and requires court approval** | OLA allows **greater discretion**; Bankruptcy is **more restrictive** |
| **Treatment of Depositors** | U.S. depositors have **priority over non-U.S. depositors and debt holders** | All depositors (U.S. and non-U.S.) have **priority under deposit insurance** | OLA gives **unequal treatment** (U.S. vs. non-U.S.); Bankruptcy treats **all deposits equally** under FDIC insurance |
| **Loss Allocation** | Shareholders and creditors of failed entity **bear losses** | Creditors generally recover in order of priority | OLA shifts risk to **private parties**; Bankruptcy provides **some recovery** |

> 💡 **Key Takeaway**: OLA is designed for **speed and stability** in systemic crises, sacrificing some creditor fairness. Bankruptcy is designed for **fairness and legal process**, with more predictable outcomes.

---

### ✅ Contrast 2: **Interchange Fee Regulation (EU) vs. U.S. (No Federal Cap)**  
*(Payment Network Pricing)*

| Feature | **EU Interchange Fee Regulation** | **U.S. (Current Status)** | **Contrast** |
|--------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------|-------------|
| **Fee Caps** | **Yes** – caps on interchange fees (e.g., 0.25%–0.40%) | **No federal cap**; fees set by market or contract | EU imposes **price controls**; U.S. allows **market-driven pricing** |
| **Merchant Surcharging** | **Permitted** in some Member States | **Prohibited in many states**, overturned in others | EU allows **surcharging**; U.S. is **mixed and evolving** |
| **Impact on Revenue** | Downward pressure on **merchant discount rates** | No direct cap; but **competitor pricing** may reduce margins | EU regulations **directly reduce revenue**; U.S. impact is **indirect** |
| **Business Strategy** | Led to **exit from EU/Australia** (e.g., card network businesses) | No forced exit; but **revenue pressure** exists | EU regulation forces **strategic retreat**; U.S. adapts through **market competition** |
| **Regulatory Oversight** | Strong, centralized, and **enforced by national regulators** | Fragmented; state-level rules vary | EU has **coordinated, uniform enforcement**; U.S. is **decentralized** |

> 💡 **Key Takeaway**: EU regulation **directly controls pricing**, while U.S. pricing is **market-based**, leading to different business strategies and revenue models.

---

### ✅ Contrast 3: **Data Privacy (GDPR) vs. U.S. (GLBA & State Laws)**  
*(Personal Data Handling and Compliance)*

| Feature | **EU GDPR** | **U.S. (GLBA + State Laws)** | **Contrast** |
|--------|------------|-------------------------------|-------------|
| **Scope** | Applies to **any company processing EU residents’ data**, regardless of location | Applies only to **U.S.-based entities** or those with U.S. operations | GDPR has **extraterritorial reach**; U.S. is **geographically limited** |
| **Penalties** | Up to **4% of global annual revenue** | Varies by state; often **fines tied to specific violations** | GDPR penalties are **proportionally severe** and **global** |
| **Data Transfer Rules** | Requires **adequate safeguards** for cross-border transfers (e.g., SCCs, adequacy decisions) | No uniform rule; **state laws may impose stricter rules** | GDPR creates **barriers to data flow**; U.S. has **more flexibility** |
| **User Rights** | Strong rights: access, erasure, portability, objection | Limited rights; **state laws vary** (e.g., CCPA) | GDPR offers **comprehensive consumer rights**; U.S. is **fragmented** |
| **Enforcement** | **EU Data Protection Authorities (DPAs)** enforce directly | Enforcement by **federal agencies (e.g., CFPB)** or **state attorneys general** | GDPR has **centralized, powerful enforcement**; U.S. is **decentralized and reactive** |

> 💡 **Key Takeaway**: GDPR is **strict, comprehensive, and globally applicable**; U.S. laws are **fragmented, state-dependent, and less punitive**.

---

### ✅ Contrast 4: **AML/CFT (U.S. Patriot Act) vs. EU Directives**  
*(Anti-Money Laundering Compliance)*

| Feature | **U.S. (Patriot Act + AMLA)** | **EU (5th & 6th AML Directives)** | **Contrast** |
|--------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------|
| **Legal Basis** | Centralized under **U.S. Treasury (FinCEN)** | Transposed into **national laws** by individual EU countries | U.S. has **centralized authority**; EU is **decentralized** |
| **Reporting Requirements** | Mandatory **CFT reporting** via FinCEN; real-time monitoring | National-level reporting; varies by country | U.S. has **uniform, centralized reporting**; EU is **country-specific** |
| **Enforcement** | FinCEN and DOJ enforce; **fines and penalties** | National authorities enforce; **fines vary** | U.S. has **stronger, coordinated enforcement** |

| **Scope** | Applies to **all financial institutions** | Applies to **banks, payment services, etc.** across sectors | U.S. has broader, more integrated coverage |

> 💡 **Key Takeaway**: U.S. AML framework is **more modern, centralized, and proactive**; EU system is **decentralized and slower to adapt**.

- **Contrast mapping** helps distinguish **similar-sounding rules** (e.g., "resolution of failure") by highlighting **functional differences**.

When studying complex regulatory environments:

text: Under Delaware corporate law, interested director transactions are permissible and not legally voidable if either a majority of disinterested directors or a majority in interest of holders of shares of the corporation’s capital stock entitled to vote approve the transaction, or if the transaction is determined to be fair to the corporation at the time it is authorized, approved, or ratified by the board of directors, a committee thereof, or the shareholders. A transaction is not voidable and a director is not accountable for failure to disclose an interest if it is confirmed by a special resolution of shareholders (requiring a two-thirds majority of those voting) and the nature and extent of the director’s interest are disclosed in reasonable detail in the notice of the meeting. Although a court may order a director to account for any profit, it will not set aside a transaction unless it is satisfied that third parties acting in good faith would not be unfairly prejudiced and the transaction was not reasonable and fair in the interests of the company at the time. Cumulative voting for director elections is not permitted under Delaware law unless specifically provided for in the corporation’s certificate of incorporation. The certificate of incorporation may allow shareholders of any class or series to vote cumulatively at all or specified elections. Under Delaware law, unless otherwise provided, shareholder actions at annual or special meetings may be taken by written consent of holders of outstanding stock with at least the minimum votes needed to pass the action at a meeting, provided all shareholders entitled to vote are present and vote; consents must be dated and collected within 60 days of the earliest dated consent. A merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all assets of a Delaware corporation must be approved by the board and a majority of outstanding shares entitled to vote. Under Jersey law, a merger or consolidation of two or more companies requires the directors of each constituent company to enter into and approve a written merger agreement (in certain circumstances), which must be authorized by a special resolution of shareholders (requiring at least two-thirds of votes cast at a quorate meeting or a higher threshold as set in the articles). Dissenting shareholders of a Jersey company have no appraisal rights and cannot receive payment in cash for the judicially determined fair value of their shares, though they may object to a merger on grounds of unfair prejudice. If a person makes an offer to acquire 90% or more of a company’s outstanding shares not already held and acquires or agrees to acquire those shares, the person is entitled (and may be required) to acquire the remaining shares, and a holder of remaining shares may apply to the court for an order that the offeror not be entitled to purchase their shares or that they be purchased on different terms. If a company, its creditors, or shareholders propose a compromise or arrangement, the Jersey courts may order a meeting of creditors or shareholders (75% in value or 75% in voting rights) to be called, and any such compromise approved by a majority in number and value or voting rights (as applicable) and sanctioned by the court is binding on the company and the relevant parties. The court may, in its discretion, treat a single class of shares as multiple or multiple classes as a single class for shareholder approval purposes, considering all relevant circumstances. Jersey law contains no specific restrictions on directors’ powers to dispose of company assets, but directors must act with care, in good faith, for a proper purpose, and in the best interests of the company. Directors are elected by a plurality of votes of shares entitled to vote and may be removed with or without cause (except in a classified board where removal without cause is only permitted if the certificate of incorporation provides otherwise), and require majority approval of outstanding shares. A director of a Delaware corporation has a fiduciary duty to the corporation and shareholders, consisting of a duty of care (to act with the care of a prudent person and disclose material information) and a duty of loyalty (to act in the best interests of the corporation, avoid conflicts of interest, and not use corporate position for personal gain). A director must not engage in self-dealing and must disclose any interest in a transaction that conflicts or may conflict with the company’s interests. Actions of directors are presumed to be made in good faith and in the best interests of the corporation, but this presumption may be rebutted by evidence of a breach of fiduciary duty. If such evidence exists, the director must prove the procedural fairness and that the transaction was fair to the corporation. A director with a material interest in a board matter may attend and be counted in a quorum but may not vote on the matter and the chairperson’s decision is final. Delaware law allows a corporation to include provisions in its certificate of incorporation to limit the personal liability of directors and officers for monetary damages arising from breaches of fiduciary duty, except for breaches of loyalty, intentional misconduct, or unlawful dividends, stock purchases, redemptions, or transactions involving improper personal benefit. These provisions do not bar claims under U.S. federal securities laws. Delaware corporations may indemnify directors and officers against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements incurred in defending actions if they acted in good faith and in the best interests of the corporation, or if they had no reasonable cause to believe their conduct was unlawful. A Delaware corporation may also indemnify against losses arising from proceedings where the person is acquitted or receives a favorable judgment, where proceedings are discontinued or settled on terms that result in benefit or detriment to the person, or where the person acted in good faith with a view to the company’s best interests. Jersey law does not permit companies to limit director liability for breaches of fiduciary duty, though a Jersey company may exempt directors and officers from liability and indemnify them for liabilities such as defending civil or criminal proceedings where they are acquitted or receive a favorable judgment, where proceedings are discontinued or settled on terms involving benefit or detriment, or where the person acted in good faith with a view to the company’s best interests, or where the company maintains insurance for persons other than directors. Amcor’s Articles of Association require full indemnification of officers against all losses, liabilities, costs, and expenses incurred as directors or officers of Amcor or related bodies. Under Delaware law, a corporation may vary the rights of a class of shares with the approval of a majority of outstanding shares of that class, unless the certificate of incorporation provides otherwise. Under Jersey law, if Amcor’s share capital is divided into more than one class, rights may be varied (i) with written consent of two-thirds of the shares of the class or (ii) by a special resolution passed at a separate meeting of the holders of the class. Shareholders in a Delaware corporation may, under certain circumstances, receive appraisal rights to receive cash equal to the fair value of their shares as determined by a court in lieu of the consideration they would otherwise receive in a major corporate transaction. Under Jersey law, dissenting shareholders have no appraisal rights, though they may object to a merger on grounds of unfair prejudice and the court may specify terms of acquisition different from the offer (including price or form of consideration). Class actions and derivative actions are generally available to shareholders of a Delaware corporation for breaches of fiduciary duty, corporate waste, or actions not taken in accordance with law, and the court may allow recovery of attorneys’ fees. Under Jersey law, a shareholder may apply to court for relief if the company’s conduct is “unfairly prejudicial” to shareholders, and the court may make orders to regulate company affairs, require the company to cease an act, authorize civil proceedings, or require the purchase of shares. Customary personal law may also provide derivative or other actions against directors or the company. In principle, Amcor will be the proper plaintiff and a class or derivative action may not be brought by a minority shareholder, though a minority shareholder may seek special dispensation from the court if they can show there are wrongdoers in control, those wrongdoers are using power to prevent action, the wrongdoing is unconscionable and oppressive, or in certain limited circumstances. Unless otherwise provided by Jersey law or by the Board, the Royal Court of Jersey is the sole and exclusive forum for derivative actions, claims of breach of fiduciary duty by directors or officers, claims against Amcor or its officers under the Jersey Companies Law or Articles of Association, or claims governed by the internal affairs doctrine, which may limit a shareholder’s ability to bring claims in a more favorable forum and discourage litigation. All shareholders of a Delaware corporation have the right, upon written demand, to inspect or obtain copies of the corporation’s shares ledger, books, and records for purposes reasonably related to their interest as shareholders. The register of directors and secretaries must be accessible during business hours, subject to reasonable restrictions. Shareholders of Amcor have the right under Jersey law to inspect the register of shareholders and, under certain conditions, obtain a copy, and to inspect the minutes of any shareholder meetings.

text: Materials, equipment, and other supplies can negatively impact Amcor’s ability to supply products to customers. Climate change may reduce agricultural productivity, leading to availability and price challenges for agricultural commodities, which could affect demand for Amcor’s products. For example, in fiscal year 2023, adverse weather in the United States reduced cattle herds, causing meat prices to rise and resulting in lower meat packaging sales volumes. The potential magnitude of these commercial risks on Amcor’s business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows cannot be predicted. The insolvency or contractual default by any of Amcor’s customers, suppliers, or financial institutions—such as banks or insurance providers—could materially harm operations and financial condition, especially during periods of economic volatility, such as that caused by the Russia-Ukraine conflict. If a counterparty defaults on a payment obligation, Amcor may be unable to collect the owed amounts, which could require write-offs. If a counterparty becomes insolvent or fails to meet obligations related to a project, Amcor may need to find a replacement or fulfill the obligations itself, which would likely be more expensive. These risks could have a material adverse effect on Amcor’s business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows, potentially leading to a competitive disadvantage. Health crises, including pandemics, epidemics, or disease outbreaks like COVID-19, may disrupt operations through temporary facility closures, supply chain interruptions, customer shutdowns, volatility in raw material costs, and labor shortages, with broader global economic or geopolitical implications. For instance, in the first half of fiscal year 2023, the Chinese government imposed sporadic COVID-19-related lockdowns, reducing demand for Amcor’s products and disrupting global supply chains. While protocols exist to manage such impacts, the extent of health crisis effects on Amcor’s business and financial results remains unknown and could be material. Amcor’s success depends on its ability to attract, develop, and retain skilled and diverse personnel in its global executive management and operations. Although Amcor has implemented talent acquisition, onboarding, and leadership programs to align new hires with company values, failure to successfully transition key hires or retain skilled personnel could disrupt strategic execution, hinder performance objectives, and impact business continuity. Regional labor shortages, wage inflation, a competitive labor market, and demographic changes pose ongoing challenges. While Amcor has managed past labor shortages and succession planning, there is no assurance it can manage future labor issues or recruit, develop, assimilate, motivate, and retain employees who uphold company culture. Amcor is subject to environmental, health, and safety (EHS) laws and regulations in all countries where it operates, as well as local and international standards for healthcare and food packaging products. Compliance requires significant financial and human resources. Changes in workplace health and safety laws or environmental regulations—such as those related to air, soil, water quality, and climate change—can increase operational costs. Amcor may face environmental liabilities for contamination at owned, used, or operated facilities, including future acquisitions, and could be subject to fines, penalties, or mandated remediation programs requiring substantial capital expenditures. Past and future environmental fines, legal costs, damage to natural resources, lost property values, and toxic tort claims may occur. Provisions are made when it is probable that liability exists and the amount can be reasonably estimated, but actual liabilities may exceed these provisions due to the difficulty in assessing long-term environmental damage. As a result, additional charges could arise, adversely affecting operating results and financial position. Climate change and greenhouse gas emissions may negatively impact Amcor’s business, with governmental bodies considering or introducing regulatory changes that could materially affect operations or financial results. Amcor is also exposed to labor disputes and the inability to renew collective bargaining agreements at acceptable terms. Approximately 45% of its employees are covered by such agreements, and although no significant labor disputes have occurred recently, isolated work stoppages have happened. Future labor disputes, including strikes or protests, could disrupt operations and harm business performance. Amcor may also fail to renegotiate agreements at acceptable terms, despite generally good employee relations. Disruptions from labor disputes among suppliers, customers, or other parties could also affect operations. Climate change poses risks through natural disasters such as snowstorms, extreme heat, hurricanes, flooding, forest fires, deforestation, loss of biodiversity, earthquakes, and drought, which could physically damage facilities, workforce, inventory, suppliers, and equipment, leading to unplanned downtime and unabsorbed costs. Climate change may also result in higher insurance premiums or the inability to insure certain risks. Long-term climate patterns could alter customer demand, especially among those relying on weather-affected supply chains, such as agricultural supply chains impacted by drought or flooding, or coastal customers affected by frequent flooding. Amcor faces cybersecurity risks from increased cyber-attacks—including computer viruses, ransomware, unauthorized access, phishing, hacking, and advanced persistent threats—by nation-state actors, criminal enterprises, individuals, or other threat groups. These risks are heightened by geopolitical turmoil, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict, increased work-from-home arrangements, and interconnected networks. Although Amcor has operational safeguards like employee training, network monitoring, strong data protection, and upgraded security systems, these measures cannot eliminate the risk entirely. Past and ongoing attacks may still impact systems, and business recovery protocols may not succeed, leading to material adverse effects on financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows. Customers, suppliers, and third-party service providers are also vulnerable to cyber-attacks, which could reduce demand for Amcor’s products or limit supply. Amcor holds sensitive, confidential, or personal data subject to privacy and security laws, which are evolving, especially in the U.S., Europe, and China, increasing compliance complexity and costs. Despite efforts to protect data, breaches, misplaced or lost data, programming or user errors, and malicious or accidental destruction could compromise data, lead to improper system use, and result in damages, disruptions, shutdowns, transaction errors, loss of customers, violations of privacy laws, regulatory fines, penalties, reputational damage, and compensatory payments—all of which could materially harm business and financial performance. Information technology failures or disruptions—due to power outages, software or hardware failures, cyber-attacks, natural disasters, telecommunications failures, user errors, unauthorized access, or catastrophic events—could compromise data, disrupt operations, and affect business performance. While Amcor has established and regularly tests a business disaster recovery plan, there is no guarantee it will resolve disruptions promptly. Such failures could lead to material adverse effects on business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows. Rising interest rates increase borrowing costs on variable-rate debt. As of June 30, 2023, approximately 30% of Amcor’s indebtedness was subject to variable interest rates. Higher inflation in Europe and the U.S. led central banks to raise interest rates during fiscal year 2023, increasing Amcor’s interest payments and potentially reducing the attractiveness of cash management programs like customer and supply chain finance, which could negatively impact cash and working capital and increase borrowings. Amcor manages interest rate exposure through a mix of fixed- and variable-rate debt, monitoring global rates, and using derivative instruments. However, if these instruments are ineffective, if Amcor is under-hedged, or if a hedge provider defaults, it could materially harm business, financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows. Continued interest rate increases could also raise the cost of obtaining new debt or refinancing existing debt. As of June 30, 2023, Amcor had $6.7 billion of debt outstanding and $1.3 billion of a $3.8 billion revolving credit facility undrawn, and it is not restricted from incurring additional debt. Amcor’s ability to service debt depends on generating sufficient cash flows, which are influenced by economic and competitive conditions and factors beyond its control. If cash flows are insufficient, financial condition and results of operations would be materially harmed. Amcor funds operations through cash from operations, commercial paper, bank term loans, committed and uncommitted credit facilities, debt issuances, and equity issuances. Credit rating agencies assess debt based on financial performance, industry outlook, and global economic conditions. Additional debt could negatively affect credit ratings, with potential outcomes including downgrades, placement on a watch list, or reduced access to capital markets, higher borrowing costs, or increased credit spreads. In addition, a significant number of Amcor’s operating subsidiaries are not guarantors of its debt. If any non-guarantor subsidiary becomes insolvent, liquidates, reorganizes, dissolves, or winds up, its assets will satisfy claims of its creditors, and there are no direct obligations to pay Amcor’s debt. Claims against such subsidiaries are structurally subordinated to all claims of their creditors. Amcor is exposed to foreign exchange rate risk, both transactional and translational. Transactional exposures arise from operations in currencies other than the entity’s functional currency, while translational exposures result from exchange rate fluctuations when converting functional currencies to U.S. dollars, affecting reported asset and liability values, income, and expenses. Movements in the exchange rates of the Euro, the United Kingdom Pound Sterling, the Swiss Franc, the Australian Dollar, the Chinese Yuan, and the Brazilian Real against the U.S. dollar may impact translational exposure. Exchange rates may change rapidly due to various factors. Amcor has recognized foreign exchange losses related to currency devaluation in Argentina, which is designated as a highly inflationary economy under U.S. GAAP.     - Well capitalized → CET1 ≥ 6.5%, Tier 1 ≥ 8.0%, Total ≥ 10.0%, Leverage ≥ 5.0%
    - Undercapitalized → progressively more restrictions
  - Restrictions include:
    - Prohibition on accepting brokered deposits
    - Prohibition on offering interest rates above market
    - Restrictions on capital distributions

> 🔍 *Key takeaway: Dividends and distributions are tightly controlled. Poor capital = loss of flexibility and access to capital markets.*

---

## 🟪 **Purple: Regulatory Oversight & Compliance Framework**  
*(Broader regulatory environment, enforcement, and compliance risks)*

- **Regulatory Oversight Bodies:**
  - **Federal Reserve**: Comprehensive supervision, stress testing, capital rules, enforcement
  - **OCC**: Supervises AENB (bank subsidiary)
  - **CFPB**: Rules and enforcement on consumer financial products and payment networks

- **Regulatory Environment:**
  - Global trend toward stricter oversight of payment networks and consumer financial products
  - Ongoing legislative and regulatory changes → unpredictable impact on business

- **Compliance Risks:**
  - Internal and external reviews for errors, misconduct, or control failures
  - Regulatory actions: investigations, fines, civil penalties, inquiries
  - Public scrutiny can expand investigations

- **Financial Holding Company Status:**
  - Requires:
    - Company and AENB to be “well capitalized” and “well managed”
    - AENB to have “satisfactory” CRA rating
  - Loss of status → barred from new financial activities or acquisitions

> 🔍 *Key takeaway: Compliance is not just about rules — it’s a continuous process with real-world consequences like fines, reputational damage, and operational restrictions.*

*(Failure scenarios and resolution plans)*
